field.qualification: 22.7% is the 19th ICLS figure, which strips subsistence agricultural production out of employment — the same survey's 13th ICLS measure puts female participation at 24.4%, so part of the 'exclusion' is a definitional reclassification of unpaid farm work rather than women leaving work. It also measures participation, not idleness: the 19.86% of their time women aged 10+ give to unpaid domestic and care work is labour that the participation rate is designed not to count.
field.hook: 22.7% → four in five working-age women counted outside the labour force
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's women are economically inactive" — the 117.4m in unpaid care work and the 19.86%-vs-1.81% time split show the work is done but uncounted, and the 19th ICLS definition itself removes subsistence producers from employment.
field.deploy: Pakistan's growth ceiling is set less by capital than by who is permitted to work: the Labour Force Survey 2024-25 puts female participation at 22.7 percent, while women spend 19.86 percent of their time on unpaid care against men's 1.81 percent.

field.qualification: The 10.2% base is a narrower federal-style measure: total tax revenue including provincial taxes and the petroleum levy was already 12.3% of GDP in FY2025, so the 13% ambition is a smaller lift than 10.2%→13% implies. A ratio target is also silent on composition — it can be met by squeezing existing filers and levies rather than by taxing agriculture, which was 24.6% of value added at an effective rate near 0.3%.
field.hook: 10.2% → 11% → 13%: a decade's fiscal ambition stated in two percentage points
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's fiscal problem is overspending, not revenue" — a 10.2% ratio the government itself targets raising sits far below the ~15% state-capacity reference, and the gap is concentrated in untaxed sectors, not in outlays.
field.deploy: Fiscal capacity, not intent, is the binding constraint: the Ministry of Finance targets tax-to-GDP rising from 10.2 to 11 percent in 2025-26 and toward 13 percent, yet the IMF finds agriculture, 24.6 percent of value added, taxed near 0.3 percent.

field.qualification: This is a share of total government spending, not a rupee amount: total public spending grew over 2005-2024, so the halving of the share is consistent with local budgets rising slowly in nominal terms while everything else rose faster. The 2005 baseline is also the high point of the district-government system then in force, so the fall partly measures the dismantling of that arrangement rather than a steady two-decade slide.
field.hook: 10% → under 5%: devolution stopped at the provincial capitals
field.useAgainst: "The 18th Amendment devolved power to the grassroots" — the transfer stopped at provinces, and the local share of spending halved after it.
field.deploy: Devolution in Pakistan stopped at the provincial capitals. World Bank figures show local-government spending falling from about 10 percent of total government spending in 2005 to under 5 percent by 2024, even as provincial revenues averaged 6.5 percent of GDP over 2010-2024.

field.qualification: "Provincial revenues" here includes federal transfers under the NFC award, so 6.5% of GDP is not a measure of provincial own-source tax effort and does not show that provinces have become better tax collectors. It is also a 15-year average, smoothing over years when the ratio sat well below that line.
field.hook: 6.5% of GDP → provinces gained revenue; federal spending never made room
field.useAgainst: "Provinces are fiscally starved under the current arrangement" — provincial revenues rose from under 4% to about 6.5% of GDP; the unresolved half of the problem is federal expenditure that did not shrink.
field.deploy: Transferring revenue is not the same as transferring obligations: provincial revenues averaged about 6.5 percent of GDP over 2010-2024, up from under 4 percent, yet World Bank analysis finds federal expenditure did not decline commensurately.

field.qualification: Recurrent spending is mostly teacher, health-worker and police salaries, so a high recurrent share is not by itself waste — an under-staffed school system needs recurrent money. What the figure indicts is the allocation rule, not the category: districts got budgets by historical precedent rather than by measured poverty or service gaps. It is also a single year, FY2023, aggregated across provinces with very different fiscal profiles.
field.hook: 80% recurrent → provinces fund inputs by precedent, not gaps by evidence
field.useAgainst: "Service delivery will improve once provincial budgets are increased" — in FY2023 over four-fifths of provincial spending was already recurrent and allocated by historical habit rather than need.
field.deploy: Budget totals reveal little about whether services improve. More than 80 percent of provincial expenditure in FY2023 was recurrent, the World Bank notes, with district allocations tracking historical precedent rather than measured poverty or service gaps, alongside the IMF's findings of weak procurement controls.

field.qualification: Sixteen cities and 4.5m residents are a modest slice of Punjab's urban population, and near-tripling from a US$6.22m base leaves an absolute sum far too small to finance municipal services at scale. Because both figures are in dollars across 2017-18 to 2023-24, rupee depreciation means the local-currency increase was larger than the dollar series shows — and the reverse caution applies to reading the dollar total as real fiscal weight.
field.hook: US$6m → US$18m across 16 cities: municipal finance responds to systems
field.useAgainst: "Pakistani local governments are structurally incapable of raising their own revenue" — 16 Punjab cities nearly tripled own-source revenues once planning and performance systems were installed.
field.deploy: Where local finance has been given systems rather than slogans, it has responded: the World Bank's Punjab Cities Program reached over 4.5 million residents in 16 cities, and their own-source revenues climbed from about US$6.22 million in 2017-18 to US$17.62 million in 2023-24.

field.qualification: Because the gap is measured per hour, it cannot be explained away by women working shorter weeks — but it is an unadjusted comparison, not a like-for-like test of men and women in the same occupation with the same schooling and experience. It also only captures those in paid work, which in Pakistan excludes most women, so it describes the penalty inside employment rather than the larger penalty of exclusion from it.
field.hook: 25% less per hour → the gap survives after working time is equalised
field.useAgainst: "Women earn less mainly because they work fewer hours" — the ILO figure is hourly, so the gap persists with working time held constant.
field.deploy: Education alone will not close the gender gap, because the penalty attaches to the job rather than the hours: the ILO's 2025 analysis finds Pakistani women earning about 25 percent less per hour than men, citing discrimination, weak labour-law compliance and informal employment.

field.qualification: The 117.4m headcount counts anyone doing any amount of unpaid care or domestic work, so it measures participation, not intensity — and roughly half of it is men, which makes it a poor standalone proof of unequal burden. The inequality shows up in hours, not heads, so this figure needs a time-use companion to carry the argument.
field.hook: 117.4m in unpaid care → 66.7m of them women, on no payroll
field.useAgainst: "Most Pakistani women are economically inactive" — 66.7m women are already working, unpaid, inside the household, which is why measured participation stays low.
field.deploy: Care work is infrastructure that no budget records. The ILO counts 117.4 million people in Pakistan doing unpaid care or domestic work, 66.7 million of them women, and globally 708 million women stood outside the labour force for that reason in 2023.

field.qualification: This is a global aggregate dominated by the most populous countries, so it establishes that care constrains women's participation worldwide without showing that care is the binding constraint in Pakistan specifically. It also rests on inactive women's stated main reason for not seeking work, a self-reported category that misses women who report multiple or no reason, and it is a 2023 figure set beside Pakistani data from 2024-25.
field.hook: 708m women worldwide → care duties, not local culture alone, bar entry
field.useAgainst: "Low female employment is a peculiarly Pakistani or South Asian cultural failing" — 708m women worldwide were outside the labour force for care reasons in 2023.
field.deploy: Women's low employment is a structural constraint rather than a cultural quirk: the ILO found 708 million women worldwide outside the labour force in 2023 owing to unpaid care, the same mechanism behind Pakistan's 22.7% female participation (LFS 2024-25).

field.qualification: The 77.8% scores whether legal frameworks exist on paper, so it can improve through legislation alone while outcomes stand still; it is a de jure measure sitting next to two de facto ones. The 20.47% parliamentary share is also lifted by reserved seats filled through party nomination, which is precisely why it sits nearly four times above the 5.71% of managerial posts women win competitively.
field.hook: 77.8% on paper → 5.71% in management: law is not leverage
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's legal framework for women is broadly in place, so equality is on track" — a 77.8% de jure score coexists with women holding only 5.71% of managerial positions.
field.deploy: Legislation is the cheapest part of gender reform. UN Women's 2024 data give Pakistan 77.8% on the SDG legal-framework indicator, yet women hold 20.47% of parliamentary seats and just 5.71% of managerial posts — de jure progress far outrunning de facto power.

field.qualification: These are modelled level effects on potential output from a full reform package, not a forecast of realised Pakistani growth: 'up to 3.5%' is the ceiling of a cross-country range, and partial or sequenced reform buys proportionately less. A one-off uplift in the level of output is also not a permanent rise in the growth rate, and the estimate carries no timetable, no fiscal cost and no distributional detail.
field.hook: 3.5% and 6% → modelled reform dividend, not promised growth
field.useAgainst: 'Institutional and governance reform is administrative housekeeping with no measurable macroeconomic payoff' — the IMF puts a quantified output figure on the reform agenda.
field.deploy: If reform is treated as a cost, the arithmetic is backwards: the IMF's 2026 Pakistan staff report estimates a comprehensive structural package could lift near-term output by up to 3.5% and medium-term output by almost 6%, against PBS-reported growth of 3.70%.

field.qualification: The 0.3% is an effective rate against sectoral value added, not against taxable income: much of agriculture is subsistence and smallholder output that would fall below any realistic threshold, and farmers still bear indirect taxes through inputs, so the revenue actually recoverable is far smaller than a 24.6%-versus-0.3% framing suggests. Agricultural income tax is also a provincial subject, so the gap is a federalism and collection-capacity problem, not simply a missing federal tax.
field.hook: 24.6% of output, 0.3% taxed → the base thins where the economy is thickest
field.useAgainst: 'Pakistan's revenue shortfall is purely an enforcement failure against salaried and corporate filers' — the largest exempted base is sectoral, not evasive.
field.deploy: Pakistan's revenue problem is composition, not rates. The IMF's 2026 staff report puts agriculture at roughly 24.6% of value added but an effective tax rate near 0.3%, which explains how total tax revenue stalls at 12.3% of GDP in FY2025.

field.qualification: GTI counts deaths from incidents coded as terrorism under its own definition, which excludes conventional battle deaths, security-force operations and much communal or sectarian violence, so 1,139 is a floor on conflict fatalities rather than the total. A single annual figure also carries no trend: it proves a level of violence, not that violence is rising or falling, and it is not comparable with NACTA's 83,000 cumulative 2001-22 figure, which rests on a different methodology.
field.hook: 1,139 deaths → three lives lost every single day of 2025
field.useAgainst: 'Post-2014 operations reduced terrorism to a residual, largely historical problem' — the 2025 death toll is a live annual figure, not a legacy one.
field.deploy: Whatever gains counter-terrorism policy has banked, the human ledger remains open: the Global Terrorism Index 2026 records 1,139 terrorism deaths in Pakistan in 2025 across 1,045 incidents — a security environment of sustained attrition rather than isolated shocks.

field.qualification: An incident count treats a mass-casualty bombing and a failed roadside IED identically, and coding rules determine whether a coordinated multi-site assault is one attack or several. Read against the 1,139 deaths, 1,045 incidents means roughly 1.1 deaths per attack — evidence that the burden is high-frequency attrition against security forces and infrastructure, not the spectacular mass-casualty bombings the public narrative remembers.
field.hook: 1,045 attacks → about 1.1 deaths each, attrition rather than spectaculars
field.useAgainst: 'Terrorism in Pakistan now consists of a handful of high-profile mass-casualty attacks' — frequency, not lethality per incident, is what the data shows.
field.deploy: Frequency, not spectacle, defines the threat. The Global Terrorism Index 2026 logs 1,045 attacks in Pakistan in 2025 producing 1,139 deaths — a ratio implying constant small-scale attrition, concentrated where militancy tracks the Afghanistan-Pakistan border.

field.qualification: These are shares of national totals, not rates per capita or per district, so they reflect where attacks happen rather than how exposed a resident of either province is. The deaths share (67%) sitting below the attacks share (>74%) also means attacks outside KP and Balochistan were on average more lethal, and roughly a quarter of incidents and a third of deaths still occurred elsewhere — concentration is not exemption for Punjab, Sindh or the major cities.
field.hook: 74% of attacks, 67% of deaths → two provinces, deadlier attacks elsewhere
field.useAgainst: 'Terrorism is an evenly distributed national threat needing uniform countrywide measures' — the geography demands province-specific and border-specific responses.
field.deploy: Terrorism in Pakistan is a governance problem with a postcode. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan absorbed more than 74% of attacks and 67% of deaths in 2025 (Global Terrorism Index 2026), which is why NACTA's non-kinetic agenda centres on Balochistan reconciliation and merged-district reform.

field.qualification: 'Safely managed' is the JMP's top service rung, requiring an improved source that is on premises, available when needed and free from contamination — failing any one criterion drops a household out of the 45%. The remaining 55% are therefore not people without water; most have access that is intermittent, distant or unsafe. The contamination component is also heavily modelled, since Pakistan lacks routine nationwide water-quality testing.
field.hook: 45% → water reaches most homes, safe water reaches fewer than half
field.useAgainst: 'Pakistan's water crisis is a problem of quantity that new supply infrastructure will fix' — over half the population's failure is in service quality and safety.
field.deploy: Access statistics flatter Pakistan's service delivery only until quality is measured: the UN SDG profile finds just 45.0% of Pakistanis on safely managed drinking water in 2024, while 95.7% have electricity — the state connects households faster than it makes supply safe.

field.qualification: The indicator covers domestic wastewater only, so industrial and agricultural effluent sits outside it entirely and total untreated discharge is worse than the 61.9% residual implies. It is also a 2022 figure, two years older than the 45.0% drinking-water number, so the two cannot be quoted as a same-year snapshot of the water system.
field.hook: 38.1% treated → three in five litres of household sewage returned raw
field.useAgainst: 'Water policy means building storage and canals' — untreated return flows degrade the supply already in the system.
field.deploy: Pakistan's water crisis is as much a treatment failure as a scarcity one: the UN SDG profile records only 38.1% of domestic wastewater safely treated in 2022, while just 45.0% of the population had safely managed drinking water in 2024.

field.qualification: The denominator is decisive here: 98.1% measures withdrawals against total renewable resources net of environmental flows, most of which are transboundary Indus inflows, while the World Bank ESG series measuring withdrawals against *internal* resources reports 326%. The same country is at 98% or 326% depending on which water is counted as Pakistan's own, so the figure must be quoted with its denominator, and it should not be mixed with the 110% estimate from a different page and year.
field.hook: 98.1% → nearly every renewable drop already withdrawn, before demand grows
field.useAgainst: 'Pakistan still has headroom to expand irrigated area and industrial withdrawals' — the system is already drawing down almost all renewable availability.
field.deploy: Water scarcity in Pakistan is structural rather than cyclical. Withdrawals reached 98.1% of available resources in 2023 on the UN SDG profile, and the World Bank projects demand rising more than 50% by 2047 under 3°C warming while supply stays fixed.

field.qualification: The 19.86% is a share of the full 24-hour day (roughly 4.8 hours), not of waking or working hours, and it measures time allocated rather than burden intensity or simultaneous tasks. It is also a correlation with women's low employment, not a demonstration that care work causes it — the age floor of 10+ folds school-age girls into the same average as adult women.
field.hook: 19.86% vs 1.81% → women carry eleven times men's unpaid care time
field.useAgainst: "Women's low workforce participation reflects personal choice or cultural preference" — an eleven-to-one care-time gap means most women's hours are committed before any job offer exists.
field.deploy: Any serious attempt to raise female employment must begin inside the household, since UN Women finds women aged 10+ spending 19.86% of their time on unpaid domestic and care work against 1.81% for men, alongside female labour-force participation of 22.7% in 2024-25.

field.qualification: The 95% is a share of withdrawals, not of water's economic value or of avoidable waste: any irrigated arid-basin economy will show agriculture dominating withdrawals, so the figure alone identifies no recoverable volume. The ~4% of GDP is a modelled estimate of efficiency losses, not a sum that could be collected by shifting water out of a sector that still supplies food and rural livelihoods.
field.hook: 95% of water for 23% of GDP → inefficiency alone costs 4% of GDP
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's water crisis is fundamentally a storage shortage solvable by building more dams" — 95% of withdrawals already go to a sector where pricing, crop choice and irrigation losses determine the outcome.
field.deploy: Irrigation is where Pakistan's water reform has the most to gain, since the World Bank attributes about 95% of freshwater withdrawals to agriculture and values inefficient agricultural use at roughly 4% of GDP — in a sector worth 23.44% of GDP.

field.qualification: This is a conditional scenario under 3°C warming, not a forecast, and the alarming gap comes as much from the modelling assumption that supply stays fixed as from rising demand. "Demand" here is projected requirement under assumed cropping, population and income paths, so efficiency gains or a shift out of water-intensive crops change the number rather than the climate doing so.
field.hook: 3°C → demand up over 50% by 2047 while supply stays fixed
field.useAgainst: "Climate adaptation is an environmental concern to be addressed once growth is secured" — water demand on this trajectory constrains agriculture, energy and food supply inside one planning generation.
field.deploy: Climate adaptation is growth policy, not an environmental side-chapter. The World Bank's 3°C scenario projects Pakistan's water demand rising more than 50% by 2047 against a broadly fixed supply, with unaddressed climate and environmental damage costing at least 18-20% of GDP by 2050.

field.qualification: Both shares are proportions of a national total, so they show where violence clusters, not per-capita risk — KP and Balochistan hold a minority of Pakistan's population, which makes their intensity worse than 74% suggests while saying nothing about absolute risk in Punjab or Sindh. With 1,139 deaths across 1,045 incidents, this is a pattern of frequent low-casualty attacks rather than mass-casualty terrorism.
field.hook: 1,139 deaths, 1,045 incidents → two provinces absorb three-quarters of all attacks
field.useAgainst: "Terrorism is a uniform national threat requiring one countrywide crackdown" — over 74% of attacks concentrate in two provinces with distinct border, governance and reconciliation drivers.
field.deploy: A uniform national counterterrorism posture misreads the threat, because the Global Terrorism Index recorded 1,139 deaths across 1,045 incidents in 2025, with over 74% of attacks and 67% of deaths concentrated in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan.

field.qualification: These are one-off level effects on output conditional on comprehensive reform being fully implemented, not additions to the annual growth rate and not cumulative year after year. "Up to 3.5%" is the ceiling of a modelled range, so partial or sequenced reform delivers a fraction of it, and the estimate assumes an implementation capacity Pakistan's governance scores do not yet demonstrate.
field.hook: 3.5% near, 6% medium → reform lifts the output level, not the growth rate
field.useAgainst: "Completing stabilisation under the IMF programme will itself restore growth" — the modelled gain sits in structural reform, which stabilisation neither contains nor guarantees.
field.deploy: Stabilisation buys time but does not raise the ceiling; IMF modelling in 2026 suggests comprehensive structural reform could lift output by up to 3.5% in the near term and almost 6% over the medium term — level gains, not a new growth rate.

field.qualification: A 0.3% effective rate reflects both weak enforcement and constitutional design: agricultural income tax is a provincial subject, so the gap is partly a federal-provincial assignment failure rather than pure evasion. Much of that 24.6% of value added is smallholder subsistence income that would fall below any plausible threshold, so taxing agriculture properly narrows the revenue gap without closing it.
field.hook: 24.6% of value added, 0.3% effective rate → a quarter of the economy untaxed
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's revenue crisis is caused by punitive tax rates on those already in the net" — the same economy taxes a quarter of its value added at 0.3%, making base coverage the binding failure.
field.deploy: Pakistan's revenue shortfall is about who sits inside the net, not how high rates are: the IMF's 2026 assessment puts agriculture at roughly 24.6% of value added yet an effective tax rate near 0.3%, with the tax ratio at 12.3% in FY2025.

field.qualification: The near-tripling runs off a very small nominal base — about US$6.22m to US$17.62m across 16 cities — so inflation and rupee depreciation over 2017-24 absorb much of the apparent gain. The score of 90 against a target of 70 measures compliance with the programme's own reform indicators, not water, sanitation or transport outcomes actually experienced by the 4.5m residents.
field.hook: 90 against a target of 70 → measured incentives moved sixteen city governments
field.useAgainst: "Local government reform is structurally impossible in Pakistan" — all 16 programme cities adopted rolling plans and beat their performance target when financing was tied to measured output.
field.deploy: Devolution's fiscal retreat is not irreversible: across the sixteen cities of the Punjab Cities Program, own-source revenues climbed from about US$6.22m in 2017-18 to US$17.62m in 2023-24, and average performance scores reached 90 against a target of 70 (World Bank).

field.qualification: A rank out of 193 moves when other countries' data or estimates change, so the slide to 168th is not by itself evidence of absolute decline in Pakistani welfare. The 0.544 is an average of health, schooling and income components and hides distribution entirely — inequality adjustment removes about a third of it — so the score cannot be attributed to any single sector's failure.
field.hook: 0.544, 168/193 → only 25 countries rank below Pakistan on human development
field.useAgainst: "Restoring GDP growth has been translating into development for Pakistanis" — human development sits near the bottom of the global distribution even across growth episodes.
field.deploy: Macroeconomic stabilisation has not translated into human development: UNDP's HDR 2025 places Pakistan at 0.544 on the HDI, 168th of 193 countries, and the same report shows 33.1% of that score lost once inequality is factored in.

field.qualification: Rs2.66tn is an estimate of the value of privileges accruing to elite groups, not cash that could be seized or revenue automatically recoverable if the privileges ended. The 8% share is against 2020-21 GDP, so after intervening inflation and nominal GDP growth neither the rupee figure nor the percentage can be quoted as current.
field.hook: Rs2.66tn → eight rupees in every hundred of GDP, captured by privilege
field.useAgainst: 'Pakistan's inequality is simply a by-product of poverty and slow growth' — this shows inequality is actively produced by policy and political-economic privilege.
field.deploy: Inequality in Pakistan is manufactured rather than merely inherited. UNDP's 2020-21 estimate valued the privileges enjoyed by elite groups at Rs2.66tn, roughly 8% of GDP at the time — against the Rs716bn UNICEF records for BISP in 2025.

field.qualification: The '3 Ps' is an organising lens, not a measurement: it assigns no weight to how much of observed inequality comes from elite power versus social discrimination versus policy design. It dates from UNDP's 2020-21 work, so citing it as UNDP's current analytical position overstates it.
field.hook: Power, People, Policy → inequality as a designed outcome, not an accident
field.useAgainst: 'Inequality in Pakistan is an income-distribution problem' — the framework shows discrimination and policy structure reproduce it independently of income.
field.deploy: Read through UNDP's '3 Ps' — power, people and policy — the out-of-school gap between Balochistan's roughly 69% and Punjab's 27% looks less like a provincial accident than the residue of who holds bargaining power over public spending.

field.qualification: A four-place slide between two HDR editions is ordinal: it can occur while Pakistan's own HDI value is flat or rising, because other countries improved faster, entered the ranking, or had data revised. Rank change across editions is also not comparable when UNDP alters methodology or data vintages.
field.hook: 164 → 168 → four places lost, no proof welfare fell
field.useAgainst: 'Human development in Pakistan deteriorated because it dropped four places in the HDI' — movement in rank is not movement in the underlying value.
field.deploy: Cross-country league tables are a weak basis for policy claims: Pakistan fell from 164th of 193 in the 2023/24 Human Development Report to 168th in 2025, though rankings depend on other countries too, while the underlying value stood at 0.544.

field.qualification: The denominator is ever-partnered women and girls aged 15-49 and the window is only the previous 12 months, so it excludes lifetime exposure, never-partnered women and anyone outside that age band — lifetime prevalence in the same survey family is far higher at 24.5%. It is self-reported violence disclosed to an enumerator, so it is a floor, not a count.
field.hook: 14.5% → one in seven partnered women assaulted within a single year
field.useAgainst: 'Violence against women is a matter of isolated, sensational cases' — this establishes annual prevalence at population scale.
field.deploy: Gender-based violence is a structural rather than episodic problem: UNFPA finds 14.5% of ever-partnered women and girls aged 15-49 reported physical or sexual intimate-partner violence in the previous twelve months, while only 61,097 women appear in UN Women's police-services figure.

field.qualification: The indicator is retrospective: it asks women already aged 20-24 about marriages contracted up to a decade earlier, so it describes the past marriage behaviour of one cohort and cannot show whether girls marrying today are marrying later. 'Married or in union' also captures informal unions that never appear in nikah registration data.
field.hook: 18.3% → nearly one in five women already wed as a minor
field.useAgainst: 'Child marriage is a vanished rural custom' — nearly a fifth of the current young-adult cohort was married before 18.
field.deploy: Child marriage is best read as an intergenerational transmission mechanism, not a cultural residue: UNFPA records 18.3% of women aged 20-24 as married or in union before eighteen, and only about one in ten women aged 15-19 with a say over healthcare.

field.qualification: This measures say over three specific household decisions — own healthcare, major purchases, visits to relatives — among one narrow five-year age band, so it is a snapshot of newly-formed households rather than a measure of women's autonomy across a marriage or a lifetime. It is self-reported and says nothing about whether bargaining power rises with age, schooling or childbearing.
field.hook: 1 in 10 → nine of ten young women with no say at home
field.useAgainst: 'A girl in a harmful marriage can simply refuse or walk away' — nine in ten cannot even decide their own medical care.
field.deploy: If autonomy is the test of development, Pakistan fails it early: UNFPA finds one in ten women aged 15-19 has a say over healthcare, major purchases and visits to relatives, while UN Women puts their unpaid-care burden at 19.86% of time against men's 1.81%.

field.qualification: 40,088 is an input count of personnel trained, not an outcome: it shows nothing about whether trained officers remained in VAWG-facing posts, whether registration or conviction rates moved, or whether the same officers were counted across multiple sessions. It also covers 2021-22 initiatives, so it is dated evidence of current police capability.
field.hook: 40,088 trained → capacity purchased, effect on cases never measured
field.useAgainst: 'The Pakistani state has done nothing institutional on violence against women' — substantial capacity-building has in fact happened.
field.deploy: Training inputs have outpaced service reach: UN Women records 40,088 law-enforcement personnel trained to respond to VAWG under 2021-22 initiatives, while the six Anti-Rape Crisis Cells established in 2024 supported 1,724 women and 27 boys.

field.qualification: This is an administrative service-contact count, not a count of victims or offences: one woman visiting repeatedly can register more than once, and the number can rise purely because reporting improved while violence stayed flat. With the underlying disaggregation unpublished, case type, referral and outcome cannot be verified by anyone outside the system.
field.hook: 61,097 women reached police → one figure nobody outside can audit
field.useAgainst: 'Tens of thousands of women reaching police proves the GBV response system works' — a contact count without outcomes proves only contact.
field.deploy: A service-contact count is not a measure of institutional success: UN Women reports 61,097 women accessing police services, but with the underlying statistics unpublished, no outsider can tell whether that reflects better reporting or worse violence.

field.qualification: The 33.1% is a loss from unequal distribution across all three HDI dimensions — health, schooling and income — so a badly skewed schooling distribution can drive it even where income looks flatter; it is not a poverty headcount and names no one at the top. Because it is a relative loss, it can worsen in a year when the raw HDI of 0.544 actually rises.
field.hook: 33.1% → a third of Pakistan's human development erased in the sharing
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's core problem is slow growth — raise the average and the gains will spread on their own."
field.deploy: Aggregate averages flatter Pakistan's record. UNDP's 2025 Human Development Report puts the HDI at 0.544, but adjusting for inequality drags it to 0.364 — a 33.1% loss spread across health, schooling and income distribution.

field.qualification: GII is built from a fixed set of channels — maternal mortality, adolescent births, parliamentary seats, secondary schooling and labour-force participation — so it measures gendered deprivation in those five places, not discrimination in law, inheritance or mobility. Its rank is out of 172 countries with the required data, a smaller universe than HDI's 193, so 145/172 cannot be read against the HDI rank of 168.
field.hook: 0.536 → 145th of 172 on women's health, voice and work
field.useAgainst: "Gender is a cultural and social question, not part of Pakistan's economic development agenda."
field.deploy: If half the population is structurally excluded, no development strategy can succeed: UNDP's 2025 Gender Inequality Index scores Pakistan 0.536, ranking it 145 of 172 countries, with government figures showing postnatal care reaching only about 44%.

field.qualification: GDI is a ratio of female to male HDI, so 0.838 means women reach about 84% of male achievement — it moves when either sex's outcomes change, and would 'improve' if men's health or schooling deteriorated. It also averages all women together, concealing the gap between an urban graduate and a rural girl counted in the same figure.
field.hook: 0.838 → Pakistani women reach 84 rupees of every male development rupee
field.useAgainst: "Men and women in Pakistan now have broadly comparable life chances; the parity gap is essentially closed."
field.deploy: Progress in women's outcomes should not be mistaken for parity; UNDP's 2025 Gender Development Index of 0.838 means women attain roughly 84% of male human development, a national average that conceals the distance between urban graduates and rural girls.

draftIssues: deploy cites figures not in fact/pairs: 84

field.qualification: This is floor-level reading proficiency at a single age, measured largely among children who are enrolled — it tests whether a ten-year-old can read one age-appropriate passage, not the quality of secondary schooling or numeracy. Because the 25.1m out-of-school children are mostly outside the assessed cohort, a population-wide figure would be worse, not better, than 78%.
field.hook: 78% → four in five ten-year-olds sit in school without reading
field.useAgainst: "Get every Pakistani child into a classroom and the education crisis is solved."
field.deploy: Building more schools will not, by itself, fix the system: the World Bank finds about 78% of Pakistani ten-year-olds unable to read a simple age-appropriate text in 2025, while UNICEF counts 25.1 million children aged 5-16 outside classrooms altogether.

field.qualification: The 5–16 denominator spans primary through secondary, so the 35% is driven heavily by adolescents who left after primary, not only by children who never enrolled — and the two demand very different remedies. 'Out of school' also means outside formal schooling, and says nothing about whether the other 65% are learning anything.
field.hook: 25.1m → one in three Pakistanis aged 5–16 outside any classroom
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan has effectively achieved universal enrolment; what remains is a quality problem."
field.deploy: Pakistan's exclusion problem is as much adolescent as early-years: UNICEF's 2025 figure of 25.1 million out-of-school children aged 5-16, about 35% of the age group, spans dropout after primary as well as never-enrolment.

field.qualification: These are rates, not counts, and the two rank differently: Balochistan's 69% applies to a small child population while Punjab's 27% applies to a vast one, so the worst-excluding province is not the province with the most excluded children. Provincial averages also flatten the gap between, say, Lahore and south Punjab inside the same 27%.
field.hook: 69% vs 27% → Balochistan excludes children two-and-a-half times Punjab's rate
field.useAgainst: "A single uniform national education emergency programme will close Pakistan's schooling gap."
field.deploy: Devolved education policy must be targeted provincially rather than nationally, since UNICEF's 2025 out-of-school rates range from roughly 69% in Balochistan to 44% in Sindh, 34% in KP and 27% in Punjab — which nonetheless holds about 9.7 million excluded children.

field.qualification: Stunting is height-for-age, a cumulative record of the first 1,000 days, so today's 40% registers deprivation already inflicted and will not move in response to this year's feeding programmes. It is also distinct from acute hunger — a child can be stunted without being wasted — so the figure evidences chronic deprivation, not a present famine.
field.hook: 40% → two in five children already set back before school begins
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's learning crisis originates in the school system — bad teachers, bad curricula, bad exams."
field.deploy: Pakistan's learning crisis is nutritional before it is pedagogical: the World Bank's 2025 finding that nearly 40% of children under five are stunted sits directly upstream of the 78% who cannot read a simple text at ten.

field.qualification: This is a cross-sectional wage gap, so part of the 45% reflects who reaches secondary school at all — wealthier, urban, better-connected families — rather than what the extra schooling itself adds. It is measured on wage earners, which in Pakistan leaves out most self-employed, informal and unpaid family workers, and the 2018 base predates the subsequent inflation surge.
field.hook: 45% → secondary schooling buys nearly half again the primary-educated wage
field.useAgainst: "Education budgets are welfare consumption Pakistan cannot afford while it is consolidating fiscally."
field.deploy: Every rupee withheld from schooling is a wage forgone later. World Bank evidence cited for 2018 puts the earnings of secondary-educated workers about 45% above those with only primary schooling, a premium 25.1 million out-of-school children will never collect.

field.qualification: A treatment count measures programme reach, not prevalence: it records children admitted to services in one year and is silent on how many severely wasted children were never found or never referred, so a higher number can reflect better case-finding rather than worsening nutrition. It also captures only acute wasting, the emergency tail, while chronic undernutrition shows up instead in the ~40% under-five stunting rate.
field.hook: 304,000 treated for severe wasting → the caseload reached, not the caseload existing
field.useAgainst: "Malnutrition in Pakistan is a flood-year emergency that recedes with the water" — a standing caseload of 304,000 severe cases in a non-disaster reporting year shows it is structural, not episodic.
field.deploy: Behind the chronic figures sits an acute emergency; UNICEF treated 304,000 children for severe acute malnutrition in 2025, the visible tail of a burden whose chronic form appears in the World Bank's finding that nearly 40% of under-fives are stunted.

field.qualification: Vitamin A supplementation is a twice-yearly campaign dose, so the 37.3 million counts contacts in delivery rounds rather than children whose diets improved; it corrects one micronutrient deficiency and cannot touch caloric or protein deficits. Reach on this scale sits alongside 304,000 severe wasting admissions and ~40% stunting, which is the point: coverage and nutritional outcome are different things.
field.hook: 37.3m dosed → the state can reach almost every child when it chooses
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan lacks the administrative capacity to run universal programmes" — a campaign touching 37.3 million children in a year shows the constraint is political priority and recurrent financing, not logistics.
field.deploy: Pakistan's delivery machinery is not the binding constraint. UNICEF reached 37.3 million children with vitamin A supplements in 2025, yet the World Bank still records nearly 40% of under-fives as stunted, which suggests reach and nutritional outcome move on separate tracks.

field.qualification: The 51% girls figure is parity inside a selected intervention cohort, not in the education system, where 25.1m children remain out of school and Balochistan's exclusion rate is ~69%; targeted programmes can engineer gender balance that the national system does not produce. "Accessed" also records entry into learning or skills provision, not completion, certification, or any measured gain in climate resilience.
field.hook: 729,000, 51% girls → parity engineered inside a programme, not inside the system
field.useAgainst: "Climate adaptation, schooling and gender equity compete for the same scarce rupee" — a single programme delivered all three to 729,000 people, so the trade-off is a design failure, not a budget law.
field.deploy: Where programmes are designed for it, gender parity is achievable: of the 729,000 who accessed climate-resilient learning and skills provision in 2025, UNICEF records 51% as girls, parity a country ranked 145th of 172 on UNDP's Gender Inequality Index does not otherwise produce.

field.qualification: 71,000 adolescents set against 25.1m out-of-school children is under three in every thousand: the figure establishes that accelerated pathways work, not that they operate at the scale of the deficit. "Entered" also counts enrolment at the front door, not completion of the pathway or transition back into formal schooling or work.
field.hook: 71,000 re-entered → proof of concept against 25.1m still outside
field.useAgainst: "Out-of-school children will be absorbed once enough schools are built" — adolescents who have already aged past their grade need accelerated second-chance routes, which new classrooms alone do not provide.
field.deploy: Proof of concept is not proof of scale. UNICEF recorded 71,000 out-of-school adolescents entering accelerated learning pathways in 2025, a workable second chance set against 25.1 million children outside the classroom altogether.

field.qualification: "Basic" access is a service-level threshold about a functioning improved source, not a guarantee that the water is safe at the point of drinking or available year-round; "durable" describes the asset, not the tariff, maintenance or local capacity that keeps it working after handover. The count is also attributable to one donor-supported channel, so it measures intervention output, not national coverage.
field.hook: 865,000 given safe water → nutrition policy delivered through pipes, not clinics
field.useAgainst: "Child malnutrition is fixed by feeding and supplementation programmes" — repeated infection from unsafe water reproduces wasting and stunting faster than therapeutic feeding can clear it.
field.deploy: Extending water access does nutrition work that feeding programmes cannot. When UNICEF-supported interventions gave 865,000 people durable basic safe-water access in 2025, they were acting on the same causal chain that produces 304,000 severe-wasting admissions a year.

field.qualification: Rs716bn is a nominal allocation, so a 20% rise over 2024 is not a 20% real increase once inflation is netted out, and it may leave the per-beneficiary transfer flat or falling. An allocation is also a budget line, not disbursement: it says nothing about how much reached households, or whether targeting caught the poorest.
field.hook: Rs716bn, +20% nominal → allocation announced, not rupees in poor hands
field.useAgainst: "Fiscal consolidation has squeezed social protection out of the budget" — the BISP line rose 20% above 2024 in the middle of austerity, so protection of the poor was a choice, not a casualty.
field.deploy: Relief and privilege are budgeted in the same ledger. UNICEF reports BISP's 2025 allocation at Rs716bn, 20% above 2024, while UNDP's 2020-21 estimate put elite-group privileges at Rs2.66tn, about 8% of GDP.

draftIssues: deploy cites figures not in fact/pairs: 21

field.qualification: A wallet is an access channel, not control: opening accounts for a million women records a change in payment mode, not whether she, rather than a male relative, holds the handset, the PIN or the decision over the money. It is also a count of women supported through one expansion, against a Gender Inequality Index of 0.536 that the delivery change leaves untouched.
field.hook: 1m women given wallets → payment rails changed, bargaining power unproven
field.useAgainst: "Women's financial exclusion is a cultural problem the state cannot reach" — switching the payment instrument moved a million women into accounts in their own name without waiting for norms to shift.
field.deploy: Delivery reform can move faster than the inequality it sits inside: UNICEF reports one million women brought into digital wallets in 2025, even as UNDP's 2025 Gender Inequality Index still places Pakistan at 0.536, ranked 145 of 172.

field.qualification: 110,000 is throughput of one interoperable registration channel, not national birth-registration coverage, and children registered this way are a small share of any year's births. Registration confers legal identity, which is a precondition for schooling, transfers and health entitlements — it is not evidence that any of those services subsequently arrived.
field.hook: 110,000 registered → legal identity, the entry ticket to every later entitlement
field.useAgainst: "Civil registration is administrative housekeeping, separate from poverty policy" — an unregistered child cannot be targeted by BISP, enrolled, or counted in the denominators that drive budgets.
field.deploy: Identity is the precondition Pakistan's service delivery keeps tripping over — UNICEF logs 110,000 children registered in 2025 through NADRA-linked, health-interoperable systems, a thin channel beside the 37.3m children the same agency reached with vitamin A that year.

field.qualification: NEET is a status category, not a measure of joblessness: it folds together young women kept out of work by care and mobility norms, discouraged workers, and those who left school early, so it does not show that 37% are actively seeking jobs. It also covers only ages 15-24, a narrower band than the 15-29 cohort usually invoked in youth-bulge arguments.
field.hook: 37% → more than a third of 15-24s neither learning nor earning
field.useAgainst: "Unemployment is only around 7%, so Pakistan's youth are broadly absorbed into work" — the unemployment rate counts only active jobseekers and misses the NEET population entirely.
field.deploy: Pakistan's youth problem is disengagement rather than measured joblessness, since the World Bank's 2025 poverty assessment finds around 37% of 15-24-year-olds outside education, employment or training while the Economic Survey's unemployment rate moved only from 6.3% to 7.1%.

field.qualification: The series ends at 2018-19 and is measured against the national poverty line, so it captures nothing of COVID, the inflation surge, the 2022 floods or the macro crisis; by 2023-24 the World Bank put about 60.4m Pakistanis below that line. A falling rate also masks the absolute count, since population grew throughout the same period.
field.hook: 64.3%→21.9% → poverty cut by two-thirds, but the series stops at 2018-19
field.useAgainst: "Poverty in Pakistan has only ever deepened and no policy has ever moved it" — the 2001-02 to 2018-19 record shows large-scale reduction did happen.
field.deploy: Nothing about Pakistan's poverty trajectory is fixed in either direction: World Bank data show the national poverty rate falling from 64.3% in 2001-02 to 21.9% in 2018-19, then reversing hard enough to leave roughly 60.4m people below that line by 2023-24.

field.qualification: This is a decomposition of where past income growth came from, not a verdict on job quality: the same assessment finds that shift went largely into low-productivity construction, trade, transport and services, with over 85% of employment informal. It explains the pre-2019 decline, and evidently did not make households resilient to the shocks that began in 2020.
field.hook: Principal driver → poverty fell on wages earned off the farm, not transfers
field.useAgainst: "Poverty reduction in Pakistan is mainly the work of cash transfer programmes" — the long-run driver identified is labour income, not social protection.
field.deploy: Pakistan's long-run poverty decline rested on a narrow foundation. The World Bank's 2025 assessment identifies rising non-agricultural labour income as its principal driver, yet the same report finds more than 85% of employment informal, rising above 95% among the poorest.

field.qualification: The unit is the household and the threshold is "some" income, so a single member driving a rickshaw counts the whole household as non-agricultural; it says nothing about what share of household earnings that is, or whether the work is steady. It is also a 2018 snapshot, taken before the post-2020 shocks reshaped labour markets.
field.hook: Three-quarters → most households already have one foot off the farm
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan remains an essentially agrarian society where households live off the land" — by 2018 most households already drew some income from outside agriculture.
field.deploy: Long before the recent shocks, the farm had ceased to be the typical household's only income source, with the World Bank finding about three-quarters of households earning some non-agricultural labour income by 2018 and its 2023 satellite analysis placing 88% of Pakistanis in city-like settlements.

field.qualification: Low productivity relative to manufacturing does not mean these jobs paid worse than the farm work they replaced — this is the very shift the World Bank credits with driving the long-run poverty fall. The claim is about the composition and productivity level of the destination sectors, not that structural change was a mistake.
field.hook: Construction, trade, transport → exit from farming without the productivity jump
field.useAgainst: "A rising services share of employment shows Pakistan is modernising its economy" — the shift was into low-productivity services, not high-value ones.
field.deploy: Composition changed while productivity did not. Much of the labour shift the World Bank describes in 2025 went into construction, trade, transport and other low-productivity services — the very movement it also credits with the long-run poverty decline.

field.qualification: Informality describes the employment arrangement — no contract, no registration, no social protection — not illegality or destitution; much of it is ordinary self-employment and small-firm work that generates real income. The 85% figure is a stock at one point and does not by itself show the share is worsening.
field.hook: 85% informal → job numbers with no contract, pension or protection behind them
field.useAgainst: "Creating more jobs will by itself pull Pakistanis out of poverty" — the jobs that exist already leave the poorest without stability or social protection.
field.deploy: A worker counted as employed may still have no contract, no registration and no social protection, which is the condition of more than 85% of Pakistan's workforce in the World Bank's 2025 assessment, and of over 95% among the poorest it surveyed.

field.qualification: Four shocks arrive together — pandemic, inflation, floods and macro stress — so this cannot apportion weight to any one of them, and analysts who blame the floods alone miss that the turn began around 2020. The reversal is also largely modelled forward from the 2018-19 survey baseline rather than directly measured year by year.
field.hook: 2020 → the year two decades of poverty reduction started running backwards
field.useAgainst: "The 2022 floods explain Pakistan's recent rise in poverty" — poverty had already begun rising around 2020, before the floods.
field.deploy: The collapse in poverty from 64.3% in 2001-02 to 21.9% in 2018-19 bought Pakistan no insurance: the World Bank finds poverty climbing again from around 2020 as COVID, inflation, floods and macro stress landed together.

field.qualification: This is an estimated additional flow into poverty attributable to one event, not a surveyed headcount, and it overlaps the broader post-2020 rise driven by COVID, inflation and macro stress — stacking it on top of those figures double-counts the same households. It also says nothing about how many recovered afterwards.
field.hook: 13m → one flood season pushed a Punjab-city's worth of people under
field.useAgainst: "Climate change is an environmental file, separate from the poverty and growth agenda" — a single climate event moved the national poverty count directly.
field.deploy: Any poverty target drafted without a flood contingency is a forecast rather than a plan, given that the World Bank estimates the 2022 floods alone pushed a further 13 million Pakistanis into poverty.

field.qualification: 1,724 is a count of people who reached a service point in six cells during one year, not a count of cases prosecuted or convicted — it measures access, not justice delivered. Set against the roughly 14.5% of ever-partnered women reporting intimate-partner violence in a single twelve-month period, six cells is a pilot footprint in a country of provinces, not national coverage.
field.hook: 1,724 survivors, six cells → a working pilot, not a national protection system
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's response to sexual violence exists only on paper" — a funded, integrated medico-legal/psychosocial/legal model is already operating and can be costed and scaled.
field.deploy: The binding constraint is delivery rather than legislation, as UNFPA's finding of weak implementation despite pro-women legal frameworks suggests; UN Women's six Anti-Rape Crisis Cells, established in 2024, reached 1,724 women and 27 boys with medico-legal, psychosocial and legal support.

field.qualification: An "active account" records a product held in a woman's name; it does not record who decides what leaves it, and many such accounts originate in transfer or digital-wallet enrolment rather than earned income. With only about one in ten women aged 15-19 reporting a say over major purchases, account ownership and financial control are separate variables that this figure collapses into one.
field.hook: 37m women's accounts → a name on the ledger, not a hand on the money
field.useAgainst: "Pakistani women are almost entirely outside the formal financial system" — ownership has moved at scale even where earning and decision-making have not.
field.deploy: Inclusion metrics and agency metrics must be read together. UN Women's 2025 results record 37 million active women-owned bank accounts in Pakistan, yet UNFPA finds only about one in ten women aged 15-19 has a say over major purchases.

field.qualification: This 12.3% is the broad measure — provincial taxes and the petroleum development levy included — so it is not the FBR-only ratio quoted in government targets, and citing them interchangeably inflates or deflates the picture by roughly two points. A headline ratio also conceals composition: agriculture is about 24.6% of value added at an effective rate near 0.3%, so the shortfall is where the base sits, not simply how much is collected.
field.hook: 12.3% of GDP → all taxes plus the fuel levy, not FBR's narrower number
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan collects barely 10% of GDP in tax" — that is the federal-only figure; the consolidated ratio including provinces and PDL is higher, and the real defect is base composition.
field.deploy: Domestic resource mobilisation remains the binding constraint on everything else Pakistan wants to fund. Total tax revenue, including provincial taxes and the petroleum development levy, reached just 12.3% of GDP in FY2025 on IMF figures, below the 25th percentile of peer countries.

field.qualification: 15% is an empirical regularity drawn from cross-country research on where state capacity becomes viable — the sources that publish it explicitly decline to call it a universal target, and countries clear it while still delivering weak services. Reaching it changes nothing on its own if over 80% of provincial spending is recurrent and district allocations track history rather than service gaps.
field.hook: 15% of GDP → a capacity threshold observed in research, not a finish line
field.useAgainst: "Once Pakistan reaches 15% of GDP in tax, the fiscal problem is solved" — the threshold is about capacity to spend, and spending quality is a separate failure.
field.deploy: Tax reform earns its political cost only if the money buys capacity. IMF and World Bank work published in 2026 treats roughly 15% of GDP as a state-capacity threshold, yet over 80% of Pakistan's provincial spending in FY2023 was recurrent.

field.qualification: 2.7 percentage points reads as a small number but represents roughly a fifth more revenue than Pakistan currently collects — arithmetic against a benchmark, not a revenue plan. It is silent on incidence: the same gap could be closed by squeezing the already-documented formal sector or by taxing a sector at 24.6% of value added paying about 0.3% effectively, and those are opposite political choices.
field.hook: 2.7 points short → roughly a fifth more revenue needed to reach the benchmark
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's tax shortfall is a vague governance complaint" — the gap has a measured size and a known location in the base.
field.deploy: The distance to adequacy is smaller than the politics around it suggests: IMF figures put Pakistan 2.7 percentage points below the 15% reference threshold in FY2025, a gap that could be narrowed by taxing agriculture, 24.6% of value added at roughly 0.3% effective.

field.qualification: Structural benchmarks record whether a step was taken — a governance plan published, an FBR process amended — not whether conduct changed; the same programme period still shows a governance diagnostic citing discretionary enforcement and limited transparency. "5 of 6" is also scored against benchmarks the programme itself selected, so it measures compliance with an agreed list, not the breadth of reform still outstanding.
field.hook: 5 of 6 benchmarks met → reform steps delivered, behaviour not yet moved
field.useAgainst: "Nothing in Pakistan's governance ever actually changes" — measurable commitments were met on schedule, including publication of a governance action plan.
field.deploy: Compliance with a programme checklist is not the same as changed conduct: the IMF logged five of six structural benchmarks met in its 2026 review, including a published governance plan and FBR reforms, while its 2025 diagnostic still records discretionary enforcement.

field.qualification: This is a change in statute with a commencement date, not revenue in hand — income from 1 January 2025 falls due for assessment only after that income year closes, so no collection outcome exists yet. Administration sits with provincial revenue authorities, not FBR, in a sector whose effective rate was about 0.3%, which is precisely the enforcement capacity the amendment has still to prove.
field.hook: 1 January 2025 → farm income becomes taxable on paper; collection still untested
field.useAgainst: "Agricultural income simply cannot be taxed in Pakistan" — all provinces amended their regimes with a common commencement date; the binding constraint is assessment and collection, not legal impossibility.
field.deploy: The binding constraint on Pakistan's tax base has been statutory exemption, not rate design: provincial agricultural income-tax regimes were amended to cover income from 1 January 2025 (IMF), reaching a sector whose effective rate stood near 0.3%.

field.qualification: The under-trial share is a ratio of two moving quantities — it can climb because trials conclude more slowly or convictions fall, not only because more people are detained — and a single-year headcount reveals nothing about how long any individual has waited. It is a process indicator about detention pending trial, so it says nothing about guilt, and nothing about the crime rate.
field.hook: 73.41% → nearly three in four prisoners are unconvicted, not serving sentences
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's prisons are overcrowded because the country has too much crime" — most inmates have not been convicted of anything; the bottleneck is trial delay and bail practice.
field.deploy: Pakistan's prisons are congested less by convicts than by people awaiting verdicts: NCHR data for 2024 record 74,918 under-trial prisoners, 73.41% of the total population, in a system already operating at roughly 152.2% of official capacity.

field.qualification: A rising under-trial share is a ratio within the prison population, so it can climb because convicted prisoners were released or fewer convictions were recorded, not only because more people were detained pre-trial. The 2017 figure is an approximate 'about 66%' set against a precise 2024 73.41%, so the roughly seven-point rise should be argued as a direction of travel, not a decimal-grade trend.
field.hook: 73.41% → three in four prisoners are held without any conviction
field.useAgainst: "Overcrowded prisons are a construction problem that new jails will solve" — the growth is in un-convicted detainees, so bail and case disposal, not capacity, is the binding constraint.
field.deploy: The direction of travel matters more than the decimals here: NCHR records the under-trial share rising from about 66% in 2017 to 73.41% in 2024, even as parole, probation and diversion remained underused.

field.qualification: 252.09m is a NIPS inter-censal projection, not a fresh headcount, so it inherits the assumptions of the last census rather than measuring people counted in 2025. A 2.07% national average also conceals provincial spread and says nothing about per-capita outcomes until it is set beside output, school places or job growth.
field.hook: 2.07% → roughly five million more Pakistanis to absorb every single year
field.useAgainst: "GDP growth of two or three per cent shows the economy is recovering" — against 2.07% population growth that is flat or falling income per head.
field.deploy: Headline growth flatters Pakistan because the denominator keeps moving: NIPS estimates put the population at 252.09 million in 2025, expanding 2.07% annually (Pakistan Economic Survey), against the roughly 60.4 million Pakistanis the World Bank placed below the national poverty line in 2023-24.

field.qualification: The 15-64 bracket is a birthday count, not an economic one: it includes students, homemakers, the long-term ill and everyone outside the labour force entirely, so 56.9% measures potential supply and not participation. It is also a share of a rising total, so the proportion can stay flat while the absolute number needing work grows every year.
field.hook: 56.9% → over half the country is working-age; far fewer are working
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's demographic dividend will automatically lift growth" — the dividend is conditional on absorbing those workers, not on their existence.
field.deploy: Age structure opens a window, but absorption decides what passes through it: 56.9% of Pakistan's population was aged 15-64 in 2025 (Pakistan Economic Survey), while the World Bank found more than 85% of employment informal.

field.qualification: The 15-29 band sits inside the 15-64 working-age group rather than adding to it, so it cannot be stacked on top of the 56.9% figure. A cohort share tells you how many young people exist, not their schooling, skills or employability — 26.56% is equally consistent with a skilled pipeline and with a NEET crisis.
field.hook: 26.56% → one in four Pakistanis is aged 15-29 right now
field.useAgainst: "Youth is Pakistan's greatest asset" — a quarter of the population aged 15-29 is a claim on jobs and classrooms until it is absorbed.
field.deploy: Skills provision, not the cohort's size, will decide the outcome here: 26.56% of Pakistanis were aged 15-29 in 2025 (Pakistan Economic Survey), and about 37% of 15-24-year-olds were NEET in World Bank evidence.

field.qualification: The ~19.8m increase is the arithmetic of births fifteen to twenty years earlier, already locked in before any current policy, so it measures the scale of required absorption rather than a policy failure. It counts people of working age, not jobs demanded: how many of them actually seek work depends on participation decisions, so this number is a ceiling on labour supply, not labour supply itself.
field.hook: 179.6m → nearly 20m extra working-age Pakistanis added in four years
field.useAgainst: "Unemployment is cyclical and growth will clear it" — almost 20m people reaching working age in four years is a structural absorption problem.
field.deploy: The scale of required absorption was locked in by births long before any current policy: the working-age population rose from about 159.8 million in 2020-21 to 179.6 million in 2024-25 (Pakistan Economic Survey), while employment rose only from roughly 67.25 million to 77.2 million.

field.qualification: The labour force counts anyone working or actively seeking work, so it swells both when opportunity draws people in and when household distress forces them to look for income — the direction alone does not tell you which. Note also that the 11.3m rise falls well short of the roughly 19.8m rise in the working-age population, meaning participation lagged rather than deepened.
field.hook: 83.1m → labour force grew 11.3m, barely half the working-age increase
field.useAgainst: "A growing labour force proves the economy is generating opportunity" — it grew slower than the working-age population, so most entrants stayed outside it.
field.deploy: A labour force expanding more slowly than the working-age population points to lagging participation: Pakistan's rose from roughly 71.8 million to 83.1 million between 2020-21 and 2024-25, against a working-age rise from 159.8 million to 179.6 million (Pakistan Economic Survey).

field.qualification: The roughly 9.95m added to employment counts anyone doing any work in the survey reference week, including unpaid family labour and casual informal work, so it is a headcount of work, not of productive or decent jobs. The simultaneous 1.39m rise in unemployment shows the two numbers move together: job creation here did not outrun the inflow it had to absorb.
field.hook: 9.95m new jobs → still 1.4m more unemployed than four years earlier
field.useAgainst: "Millions of jobs were created, so the employment challenge is being met" — unemployment rose by 1.39m over exactly the same period.
field.deploy: Pakistan's labour market is absorbing workers without relieving the pressure on them: the Pakistan Economic Survey records employment climbing from roughly 67.25m to 77.2m between 2020-21 and 2024-25, yet the labour force expanded from about 71.8m to 83.1m over the same period.

field.qualification: Measured unemployment requires active job search, so anyone who has stopped looking or is scraping a living in informal work is recorded as employed, not unemployed — which is why a 7.1% rate coexists with a decade of distress. The 0.8 percentage-point rise is also small relative to what it sits on top of: nearly ten million jobs were added over the same four years.
field.hook: 7.1% → the jobless rate rose even as ten million jobs appeared
field.useAgainst: "At 7.1% unemployment Pakistan's labour market is sound by regional standards" — the low rate reflects informal survival work counted as employment, not absorption.
field.deploy: A young population becomes a dividend only where demand for labour exists; unemployment in Pakistan drifted up from 6.3% to 7.1% between 2020-21 and 2024-25 (Pakistan Economic Survey), even as roughly 37% of 15-24 year-olds were NEET (World Bank, 2025).

field.qualification: The 103.5 MAF figure is a benchmark of average system *usage* — water actually diverted into the canal network — not a measure of the renewable resource, of demand, or of what is sustainable; a year hitting 103.5 MAF is normal, not adequate. It also covers surface water at canal heads only, so it hides both groundwater pumping and the losses between the barrage and the farm gate.
field.hook: 103.5 MAF → the historic norm of use, not the water the country needs
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's rivers already deliver over 100 MAF, so the problem is purely distribution" — the benchmark records what the system habitually withdraws, not what is available or sustainable.
field.deploy: Debates about Pakistani water stress need a yardstick before they need adjectives, and the Pakistan Economic Survey supplies one: normal system usage of roughly 103.5 MAF, against withdrawals already running at 98.1% of available resources (UN SDG Pakistan profile, 2023).

field.qualification: 92.0 MAF is one year's surface-water availability, and a single year cannot distinguish a dry season from a structural decline in the system. It also measures water entering the canal system, not water reaching crops, and says nothing about the groundwater pumping farmers use to cover the gap.
field.hook: 92 MAF → an unremarkable year that still ran short of the canal benchmark
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan only faces a water crisis in drought or flood years" — an ordinary year already delivered below the system's own long-run usage benchmark.
field.deploy: A system already stretched entered 2025-26 with less than it normally uses, surface-water availability recorded at about 92.0 MAF by the Pakistan Economic Survey — the base on which agriculture, 23.44% of GDP in FY2025-26, must plan.

field.qualification: An 11.1% shortfall against a long-run average is a supply deviation, not a measured crop loss — it does not tell you how much output fell, because the deficit lands unevenly across kharif and rabi and across canal commands, and tube-wells absorb part of it at the cost of aquifer depletion and diesel. A shortfall against average use is also not a shortfall against need, since the average itself embeds today's inefficient practice.
field.hook: 11.1% below average → scarcity is the baseline condition, not the emergency
field.useAgainst: "Water shortages only bite in crisis years" — even a year with no flood and no declared drought ran more than a tenth below normal system use.
field.deploy: Irrigated farming needs predictable supply as much as plentiful supply; in 2025-26 availability ran roughly 11.1% below average system usage (Pakistan Economic Survey), while the World Bank projects demand rising more than 50% by 2047 under 3°C warming.

field.qualification: 2022-23 was the year of catastrophic flooding, yet canal availability was the lowest in the series — the figure measures water Pakistan could capture and divert, not rainfall or river flow, so it indicts storage and timing rather than a shortage of precipitation. A 29.8% swing below average also means the annual average is a weak planning number for a system this volatile.
field.hook: 72.7 MAF in the flood year → too much water, too little of it captured
field.useAgainst: "The 2022 floods showed Pakistan has surplus water, only bad drainage" — the same year recorded availability nearly 30% below average system usage.
field.deploy: Volatility, not steady decline, defines Pakistan's water supply: the Pakistan Economic Survey records availability collapsing to 72.7 MAF in 2022-23, some 29.8% below average, in the same period that flooding pushed 13m people into poverty (World Bank, 2022).

field.qualification: 95% is a share of withdrawals, not of economic value: that water is attached to a sector producing under a quarter of GDP, so the ratio measures allocation, not productivity or waste per unit. It also means the arithmetic of non-agricultural conservation is trivial — even eliminating all domestic and industrial use would free only about 5% of withdrawals.
field.hook: 95% of withdrawals → 23% of GDP: the water sits where the value doesn't
field.useAgainst: "Urban wastage and leaking household taps are draining Pakistan's water" — every non-agricultural use combined accounts for roughly one-twentieth of withdrawals.
field.deploy: Any serious water strategy has to be an agricultural strategy, because the World Bank puts farming at roughly 95% of Pakistan's freshwater withdrawals — a share claimed by a sector contributing 23.44% of GDP in FY2025-26 (Pakistan Economic Survey).

field.qualification: 49,651 MW is nameplate installed capacity, which is not dependable capacity, not dispatched generation, and not delivered supply — hydel plates derate sharply in low-flow months and transmission constraints strand plants that are technically available. The figure is also silent on the two things consumers experience: tariff and reliability.
field.hook: 49,651 MW → installed on paper; the shortfall is wires, fuel and money
field.useAgainst: "Load-shedding continues because Pakistan simply lacks generation capacity" — installed capacity comfortably exceeds peak demand; the binding constraints are transmission, fuel cost and payment.
field.deploy: Pakistan's electricity crisis is not a shortage of plant: installed capacity reached 49,651 MW in FY2025-26 (Pakistan Economic Survey), enough on paper for a population NIPS estimates at 252.09m, which turns the argument towards tariffs, transmission and governance instead.

field.qualification: These are shares of installed capacity, not of generation or of system cost — thermal plants still set the marginal price and carry capacity payments whether or not they run, so a diversified plate mix does not translate into a diversified bill. Hydel's 23.4% in particular is a nameplate share that shrinks in winter low flow, exactly when demand for heating peaks.
field.hook: 49.2% thermal → the fuel import bill still sets the price of power
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's power system is overwhelmingly fossil-fuelled and has done nothing on clean energy" — hydel, renewables and nuclear together exceed half of installed capacity.
field.deploy: The plate has diversified faster than the bill: thermal still holds 49.2% of installed capacity in FY2025-26, with hydel at 23.4%, renewables 20.3% and nuclear 7.1% (Pakistan Economic Survey), yet thermal contracts continue to set the marginal price.

field.qualification: This is a nine-month (July–March) window that includes the high-flow monsoon and post-monsoon months, so it flatters hydel relative to a full-year or winter-only figure. A majority share of generation is also not a majority share of cost: thermal capacity remains contracted and paid for as the balancing and winter-peak resource.
field.hook: 53.1% → most electrons were already non-thermal, over nine monsoon-favoured months
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's clean capacity exists only on paper and rarely runs" — hydel, nuclear and renewables supplied the majority of actual generation over Jul–Mar FY2026.
field.deploy: Any claim that the transition has already arrived should be dated carefully: hydel, nuclear and renewables supplied 53.1% of electricity in July–March FY2026 (Pakistan Economic Survey), a window that includes the monsoon months when river flows are at their strongest.

field.qualification: A 23.44% share of value added is not a 23.44% share of workers or livelihoods, and because it is measured at current prices the share can rise in a year when food prices outpace prices elsewhere without a single extra tonne being produced. It also conceals composition: 62.45% of that value added is livestock, so 'a quarter of GDP is agriculture' does not mean a quarter of GDP is crop farming.
field.hook: 23.44% → a quarter of GDP, yet most of it is livestock
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan has already structurally transformed out of agriculture into services" — a sector still worth 23.44% of GDP in FY2025-26 cannot be treated as residual.
field.deploy: Agricultural policy cannot be written as crop policy. Agriculture supplied 23.44% of GDP in FY2025-26, yet livestock alone accounted for 62.45% of that value added — 14.64% of the whole economy (Pakistan Economic Survey) — so the support-price machinery reaches only a minority of the sector.

field.qualification: 2.89% is a rebound measured against an unusually weak 1.53% base year, so the acceleration flatters itself; a sector growing 2.89% against 2.07% annual population growth adds under a percentage point per head. The headline also averages a livestock sub-sector growing 3.75% with important crops at 0.65%, so 'the sector recovered' is true only in aggregate.
field.hook: 2.89% vs 1.53% → recovery only just outrunning 2.07% population growth
field.useAgainst: "Pakistani agriculture is in terminal decline" — the sector nearly doubled its growth rate year on year in FY2025-26.
field.deploy: Recovery needs a per-capita test before it counts as progress: agriculture grew 2.89% in FY2025-26 against 1.53% the year before (Pakistan Economic Survey), but with population rising 2.07% a year, the gain per Pakistani is under one percentage point.

field.qualification: This is a share of value added, not of land, water, subsidy or credit, so livestock's 62.45% dominance describes where output value sits, not where policy support goes. The share is also partly passive: with important crops growing only 0.65% in the same year, livestock's weight rises because the crop denominator is weak, not solely because herds are booming.
field.hook: 62.45% → livestock, not wheat or cotton, is agriculture's real centre of gravity
field.useAgainst: "Agricultural policy means crop policy — support prices for wheat and cotton are the sector's main lever" — that reaches barely a third of sectoral value added.
field.deploy: Where the sector's value sits and where the state spends have drifted apart: livestock now generates 62.45% of agricultural value added and 14.64% of GDP in FY2025-26 (Pakistan Economic Survey), while important crops grew just 0.65% that same year.

field.qualification: One fiscal year's growth gap is not evidence that farmers are deliberately diversifying; it is equally consistent with a poor crop year, since cotton actually fell about 0.5% in the same period. Growth rates also say nothing about who owns the animals — a 3.75% rise in livestock value added can accrue to larger herd owners rather than to the landless or near-landless rural poor.
field.hook: 3.75% vs 0.65% → herds carried the sector while crops stalled
field.useAgainst: "A bad crop year means a bad year for the whole rural economy" — livestock grew nearly six times faster than important crops in FY2025-26.
