field.deploy: Although livestock's 3.75% growth against 0.65% for important crops is often read as deliberate diversification, cotton fell about 0.5% in the same year (Pakistan Economic Survey, FY2025-26) — a gap that widens when crops fail, not only when herds prosper.

field.qualification: Production is not availability and availability is not consumption: 29.61m tonnes is national output before storage losses, procurement policy and price, and a 4.3% rise sits against 2.07% annual population growth, so the per-head gain is modest. Nearly 40% under-five stunting alongside rising wheat output shows the binding constraint is access, diet quality and disease environment, not tonnage.
field.hook: 29.61m tonnes → more wheat grown does not mean more children fed
field.useAgainst: "Child malnutrition in Pakistan is a food-production shortfall" — stunting stays near 40% in a year wheat output rose 4.3%.
field.deploy: Pakistan's nutrition crisis is a problem of access rather than harvest: wheat output reached about 29.61 million tonnes in FY2025-26, up 4.3% (Pakistan Economic Survey), while nearly 40% of children under five remain stunted (World Bank, 2025).

field.qualification: This is tonnage, not value: a 2.8% rise in output translates into export earnings only through world prices, grade and marketable surplus, none of which the volume figure captures. At 2.8% the increase also barely exceeds 2.07% population growth, so the domestic surplus available for export is not expanding as fast as the headline suggests.
field.hook: 9.99m tonnes → a 2.8% rise in volume, not necessarily in export earnings
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's exportable agricultural base collapsed along with cotton" — rice output still rose 2.8% to nearly 10m tonnes in FY2025-26.
field.deploy: Exportable surplus, not output, is the figure that matters for the trade account: rice production rose 2.8% to roughly 9.99 million tonnes in FY2025-26 (Pakistan Economic Survey), barely ahead of the 2.07% annual population growth feeding domestic demand.

field.qualification: A 0.5% fall is close to flat, so the story is persistent stagnation rather than a dramatic crash — the damage is the level cotton is stuck at, not this year's change. It is also a production figure in bales, which says nothing about lint quality, ginning losses or how much of the textile industry's raw material is now imported.
field.hook: 7.05m bales → cotton edged down while the rest of agriculture grew
field.useAgainst: "Textile export weakness is a factory-floor problem of energy costs and productivity" — the raw-material base itself shrank while agriculture overall grew 2.89%.
field.deploy: Headline agricultural recovery conceals a stalled industrial crop: cotton output slipped roughly 0.5% to about 7.05 million bales in FY2025-26 (Pakistan Economic Survey), even as overall agriculture grew 2.89%, leaving textiles dependent on a stagnant domestic supply.

field.qualification: Rs999bn is gross value added, not profit, and it is not net of feed, chick and energy costs that dominate poultry margins. The 1.5m jobs are large for one value chain but small against a labour force of 83.1m, and in an economy where over 85% of employment is informal the count says nothing about contracts, wages or security.
field.hook: Rs999bn → poultry is a near-trillion-rupee chain employing over 1.5m
field.useAgainst: "Livestock is backyard subsistence activity with no industrial scale or job-creating capacity" — one poultry chain alone generates near Rs1 trillion and 1.5m+ jobs.
field.deploy: Where agriculture diversifies, it delivers: poultry generated roughly Rs999 billion in gross value added and employed more than 1.5 million people in FY2025-26 (Pakistan Economic Survey), a meaningful if modest dent in a labour force of 83.1 million.

field.qualification: 60.4m is a headcount against the national line, so it moves with population as much as with welfare: at ~2.07% annual growth the absolute number can rise even in a year when the poverty rate is flat or falling. It also says nothing about depth — a household one rupee below the line and one at half the line count identically.
field.hook: 60.4m → poverty counted in people, not in percentage points
field.useAgainst: 'The poverty rate has come down over two decades, so fewer Pakistanis are poor today' — a falling rate against a growing base still leaves ~60.4m below the line.
field.deploy: Percentages flatter Pakistan's poverty record; absolute numbers do not. World Bank analysis places about 60.4 million people below the national poverty line in 2023-24, a figure that can keep climbing while population grows at 2.07% annually.

field.qualification: This is a ratio, not a level: double the rural rate still leaves a large absolute urban poor population, because the urban base is smaller. The split also depends on the administrative rural/urban boundary, which the Degree-of-Urbanisation evidence suggests misclassifies dense town-like settlements as rural.
field.hook: 2× → rural poverty double urban, on a boundary drawn administratively
field.useAgainst: 'Poverty in Pakistan is now essentially an urban, inflation-driven phenomenon' — the rural rate remains more than twice the urban one.
field.deploy: A nationally uniform social protection design cannot reach a poverty map this uneven: rural poverty remains more than twice urban poverty (World Bank, 2025), and district estimates stretch from roughly 3.5% in Islamabad to 76.9% in Tharparkar.

field.qualification: 3.5% and 76.9% are the two endpoints of a district distribution, not typical values — most districts sit far from both, and Islamabad is a small federal enclave whose profile no ordinary district can replicate. District-level figures in spatial analysis are small-area estimates built from survey and geographic data, not direct district censuses of the poor.
field.hook: 3.5% to 76.9% → a twenty-two-fold poverty gap inside one country
field.useAgainst: 'A uniform national cash-transfer benefit set at one level will reach Pakistan's poor' — one national parameter cannot fit Islamabad and Tharparkar.
field.deploy: Geography, not merely class, determines life chances in Pakistan: World Bank spatial analysis in 2025 found poverty as low as about 3.5% in Islamabad and as high as 76.9% in Tharparkar, with seven of the ten poorest districts in Balochistan.

field.qualification: Poorest districts are ranked by poverty rate, and Balochistan holds a small share of national population — so seven of ten poorest districts does not mean most poor Pakistanis live there. The larger absolute number of poor people sits in populous Punjab and Sindh districts with lower rates.
field.hook: 7 of 10 → poorest districts cluster in Balochistan, not most poor people
field.useAgainst: 'Balochistan's grievance is a political and security question rather than a development one' — the deprivation gap is measurable in the district rankings.
field.deploy: Balochistan's political grievances rest on measurable deprivation, not rhetoric alone: seven of the ten poorest districts identified in the World Bank's 2025 analysis lie in the province, even though most of Pakistan's 60.4 million poor live elsewhere.

field.qualification: The satellite method classifies built-up density and population grids — physical form, not urban function: a dense settlement counts as a town even with no municipal government, no municipal revenue and no piped network. The 61% figure still governs administrative status and fiscal allocation, so the gap is a budgeting problem, not just a measurement curiosity.
field.hook: 61% rural on paper → 88% already living in city-shaped places
field.useAgainst: 'Pakistan is still a predominantly rural country, so urban policy and municipal finance can wait' — most people already live at urban densities.
field.deploy: Because Pakistan budgets for the country its records describe rather than the one its people inhabit, roughly 61% was classed rural in 2023 while satellite Degree-of-Urbanisation analysis found 88% living in places physically resembling towns or cities (World Bank).

field.qualification: This is a characterisation, not a measurement: it carries no quantity, and it applies to parts of Pakistan's urbanisation rather than all of it — Karachi and Lahore are not equivalent cases. On its own it cannot show how much productivity the agglomeration failed to generate; the labour-composition and informality evidence does that work.
field.hook: 'Sterile agglomeration' → density that crowds people without compounding their productivity
field.useAgainst: 'Urbanisation is itself a growth strategy — move people into cities and productivity follows' — density without firms or services yields neither.
field.deploy: 'Sterile agglomeration' is the World Bank's 2025 verdict on parts of Pakistan's urban growth, and the labour data explain it: much of the shift out of farming went into low-productivity construction, trade, transport and services, with over 85% of employment informal.

field.qualification: An inside piped connection measures service delivery, not water safety or sufficiency: a piped household can receive contaminated or intermittent supply, while households without one may buy safe tanker or bottled water. That gap is visible in the same assessment, where roughly half of households are counted as having safely managed drinking water against only 17% with an inside pipe.
field.hook: 17% → five in six households get water from outside the home
field.useAgainst: 'Pakistan's water problem is basin-level scarcity' — the binding failure here is last-mile municipal delivery into the household.
field.deploy: Pakistan's cities have grown in population without growing in plumbing: the World Bank's 2025 assessment finds only around 17% of households have a piped water connection inside the home, even as roughly half are counted as having safely managed drinking water.

field.qualification: 'Safely managed' is a composite standard — supply on the premises, available when needed, and free from contamination — so a household can be counted as unserved for reliability alone while its water is clean. The 31% sanitation figure runs on a separate ladder and denominator, so it is not the mirror image of the water number and the two cannot be summed.
field.hook: Half safe water, 31% unsafe sanitation → coverage hides quality and reliability
field.useAgainst: 'Headline coverage figures show most Pakistanis now have water and a toilet' — half fall short once availability and contamination are counted.
field.deploy: Water and sanitation are governance questions, not environmental ones: the World Bank's 2025 baseline shows only about half of households with safely managed drinking water and 31% lacking safe sanitation, alongside 60.4m Pakistanis below the national poverty line in 2023-24.

field.qualification: The 18-20% is a no-action scenario bundling three distinct drivers — climate risk, environmental degradation and air pollution — so it cannot be cited as the cost of climate change alone, and it is not comparable to the narrower up-to-9% climate-only estimate in E467. It is a projected deviation from a counterfactual path to 2050, not a forecast that GDP will be 18-20% lower than today.
field.hook: 18-20% of GDP by 2050 → climate plus dirty air plus degraded land, combined
field.useAgainst: "Environmental protection is a luxury Pakistan can defer until it is richer" — the cost of deferral is a fifth of the 2050 economy.
field.deploy: The fiscal case for adaptation spending does not rest on future weather alone: the World Bank estimates climate risks, environmental degradation and air pollution together could cut GDP by at least 18-20% by 2050 without action.

field.qualification: The CCDR is a diagnostic and advisory report, not a budgeted programme or a binding commitment, so it evidences what the World Bank recommended in 2022 rather than what Pakistan has implemented. Its 2022 date also means it predates the NDC 3.0 targets and the later climate-finance instruments, so it cannot be cited as an assessment of current policy.
field.hook: CCDR 2022 → people-centred adaptation named the priority, not emissions cuts
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's climate response should focus on cutting its own emissions" — the Bank's country diagnostic puts adaptation and resilience first.
field.deploy: Because the damage is already in the record — the 2022 floods alone cost over US$30bn and displaced more than 8m people — the World Bank's 2022 Country Climate and Development Report urges a fundamental shift toward people-centred adaptation and resilience.

field.qualification: The 17% figure is a sectoral loss within agriculture under particular scenarios, not a 17% hit to national GDP, and the 9% is an upper bound rather than a central estimate. Both are scenario outputs on a different and narrower basis than the 18-20% combined figure in E465, so adding or conflating the two double-counts.
field.hook: 9% GDP, 17% in agriculture → the same climate shock lands twice as hard on farms
field.useAgainst: "Climate losses will be spread evenly across the economy" — agriculture absorbs roughly double the national rate.
field.deploy: Adaptation money should follow exposure rather than sector size: World Bank scenarios put climate losses at up to 9% of GDP by 2050 but as much as 17% within agriculture, which still contributed 23.44% of GDP in FY2025-26.

field.qualification: The US$30bn+ combines physical damages with wider economic losses, so it is not a reconstruction bill and should not be read as a cash requirement. The death toll and displacement counts are from a single extreme season and cannot be annualised into an expected yearly cost.
field.hook: US$30bn, 1,700 dead, 8m displaced → one monsoon, the size of a fiscal crisis
field.useAgainst: "Disaster losses are humanitarian, not fiscal" — one flood season cost more than most of Pakistan's annual development budget.
field.deploy: One season redrew Pakistan's poverty map: the 2022 floods killed more than 1,700 people, displaced over 8m and caused in excess of US$30bn in damages and economic losses, pushing an additional 13m Pakistanis below the poverty line.

field.qualification: Second-warmest in 65 years is a ranking within the length of the record, not evidence that 2025 was unprecedented, and 23.9°C is a national annual mean that flattens the heat extremes actually experienced in Sindh or southern Punjab. A single warm year is also not by itself a trend.
field.hook: 23.9°C, second-warmest in 65 years → the projection arrived inside the record
field.useAgainst: "Climate impacts are a 2050 problem for Pakistan" — the national temperature record is already being rewritten.
field.deploy: The warming Pakistan plans for has already arrived. The Economic Survey records 2025 as the second-warmest year in 65 years, averaging 23.9°C, and government data show the monsoon that followed intense heat bringing rainfall roughly 50% above average.

field.qualification: A 3% shortfall against normal is within ordinary year-to-year variation and proves nothing about drying; its value is that a near-normal national annual total coexisted with severe floods. It says nothing about where or when the rain fell, which is what determines flood damage.
field.hook: 3% below normal rainfall → the flood year that looked average on the annual sheet
field.useAgainst: "Rainfall was near normal, so 2025's flooding was not a climate signal" — the national average conceals the distribution that caused it.
field.deploy: Water-storage and drainage investment should be sized to distribution, not totals: the Economic Survey puts 2025 rainfall about 3% below normal, a near-normal year that still contained a monsoon roughly 50% above average and severe flooding episodes.

field.qualification: The ~50% above-average figure is for monsoon-season rainfall specifically, not annual rainfall, which is why it sits alongside a 3% below-normal year rather than contradicting it. "Larger local deviations" means the national figure understates what individual districts received, so it cannot be used to size damage anywhere in particular.
field.hook: Monsoon 50% above average → heat first, then the water arrives all at once
field.useAgainst: "Climate change means Pakistan will simply get less water" — the damage comes from timing and concentration, not scarcity alone.
field.deploy: National averages are the wrong instrument for sizing climate risk: the Government of Pakistan reports 2025 monsoon rainfall roughly 50% above monsoon averages, with larger local deviations, in a year the Economic Survey records as ~3% below normal overall.

field.qualification: US$500m is an allocation to one subprogram, not disbursed or absorbed spending, and it sits against adaptation needs measured in tens of billions — the 2022 floods alone cost sixty times this amount. An allocation figure also says nothing about which resilience outcomes were delivered.
field.hook: US$500m resilience subprogram → one-sixtieth of a single flood's bill
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan is now financing climate resilience at scale" — current allocations are a fraction of one disaster's losses.
field.deploy: Adaptation finance has begun to appear in the budget at meaningful scale — US$500m for CDREP Subprogram-II in 2026, per the Pakistan Economic Survey — yet that is a fraction of the US$30bn-plus the World Bank costed for the 2022 floods alone.

field.qualification: A taxonomy is a classification rulebook for what may be labelled green; issuing it moves no money and carries no disbursement figure, and Pakistan's own NDC 3.0 puts the requirement at ~US$565.7bn with two-thirds of the target conditional on external finance. Instrument creation is a precondition for climate capital, not evidence that it has arrived.
field.hook: Green Taxonomy → a rulebook for labelling capital, not capital itself
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan has no institutional architecture for climate finance and simply waits for donors" — the Green Taxonomy and climate-investment planning instruments are domestic machinery built to direct public and private capital.
field.deploy: Building the plumbing for climate capital is the easier half of the task. Pakistan issued a Green Taxonomy and climate-investment planning instruments in 2026 (Pakistan Economic Survey), yet its own NDC puts the requirement to 2035 at roughly US$565.7bn.

field.qualification: The 20x figure is a hotspot statement about the most polluted parts of the Indo-Gangetic Plains and Himalayan foothills, not a Pakistan-wide annual mean, and the benchmark is WHO's health-based guideline rather than any national standard. It measures concentration, not damage: exposure and harm depend on how many people live under those readings.
field.hook: 20x WHO limit → the safe threshold is a rounding error here
field.useAgainst: "Smog is a seasonal Lahore inconvenience that passes with the winter" — concentrations across the whole airshed sit an order of magnitude above the health-based standard.
field.deploy: Air quality here is not a matter of marginal exceedance but of an entirely different order: World Bank figures for 2025 show PM2.5 in the Indo-Gangetic Plains and Himalayan foothills exceeding the WHO safe level more than twentyfold.

field.qualification: This is a modelled counterfactual — years gained if pollution fell to the reference standard — not observed deaths, and the 3–5 year range applies to the region's worst-affected areas, not to the national average behind Pakistan's 67.8-year life expectancy. It also isolates air pollution from the water, nutrition and health-system deficits that shorten lives alongside it.
field.hook: 3–5 years → air quality moves life expectancy more than most health budgets
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's health outcomes are limited by hospitals and doctors, so spending belongs in clinical care" — ambient air costs the most polluted populations years of life before any patient reaches a clinic.
field.deploy: The damage from polluted air lands on human capital rather than hospital budgets alone, since the World Bank estimated in 2025 that it can shorten life by three to five years in the region's most polluted areas, against a life expectancy of 67.8 years.

field.qualification: Transboundary means sources and exposure are shared across a common airshed; it attributes no share to any one country or province and therefore cannot be read as evidence that Pakistan's pollution is mostly imported. The same finding that dilutes exclusive provincial responsibility also rules out blaming a neighbour, since domestic transport, industry and energy sit inside the airshed.
field.hook: One airshed → Lahore's air is partly decided outside Punjab's jurisdiction
field.useAgainst: "Punjab's own enforcement can clean Lahore's air" — pollution moves across administrative borders, so a province acting alone cannot control its own exposure.
field.deploy: Provincial smog policy will always underperform its own targets because, as the World Bank noted in 2025, pollution across the airshed is transboundary — the same finding that forbids Punjab from treating the problem as entirely someone else's.

field.qualification: The five sectors describe programme design — what the diagnosis treats as material — not measured source shares, so the fact cannot be used to say transport or industry contributes any particular percentage of PM2.5. Nor does breadth guarantee delivery: a programme spanning five sectors needs five sets of implementing agencies to act.
field.hook: Five sectors → stubble burning is one input, never the whole explanation
field.useAgainst: "Smog is caused by crop-residue burning, so a burning ban solves it" — the clean-air programme treats transport, industry, energy and municipal services as equally in scope.
field.deploy: The breadth of the Punjab clean-air programme is itself the argument: World Bank documentation from 2025 has it covering transport, agriculture, industry, energy and municipal services, which places delivery in the hands of five separate administrative machines.

field.qualification: Approval is a commitment to a single province's programme, not disbursement, spending or a measured fall in PM2.5, and its scale should be read against the US$500m national CDREP subprogram and the ~US$565.7bn NDC requirement. A financing figure records the price of one response, not the cost of the problem.
field.hook: US$300m → one province's clean air, against a US$565.7bn climate bill
field.useAgainst: "Air quality attracts talk but no financing" — a US$300m operation was approved in 2025 for Punjab's clean-air programme alone.
field.deploy: Read against the ~US$565.7bn Pakistan's NDC puts to 2035, the World Bank's US$300m approval for Punjab's clean-air programme in 2025 and the US$500m CDREP allocation show a response measured in hundreds of millions confronting a problem priced in hundreds of billions.

field.qualification: The ~35% denominator is the 5–16 age cohort specifically, so it is not a share of all children, and the indicator counts enrolment or attendance rather than learning — being counted 'in school' is compatible with the 78% of ten-year-olds who cannot read a simple age-appropriate text. Access and learning are two separate failures stacked on each other.
field.hook: 25.1m → a third of the 5–16 cohort outside any classroom
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's education problem is one of quality, since enrolment is broadly achieved" — a third of the 5–16 age group is not enrolled at all.
field.deploy: Pakistan's schooling deficit is two failures stacked rather than one: UNICEF's 2025 estimate puts 25.1 million children aged five to sixteen out of school, while the World Bank finds 78% of ten-year-olds cannot read a simple age-appropriate text.

field.qualification: These are rates — exclusion intensity within each province's own cohort — and they invert when converted to caseloads: Balochistan's ~69% is 3.5m children while Punjab's 27% is around 9.7m. Ranking provinces by rate produces a different priority list from ranking by the number of children actually out of school.
field.hook: 69% versus 27% → worst rate in Balochistan, biggest numbers in Punjab
field.useAgainst: "Out-of-school children are a Balochistan problem, so resources should follow the worst rate" — the highest exclusion rate and the largest child population sit in different provinces.
field.deploy: Any national education plan that treats exclusion as uniform will misallocate resources, since UNICEF's 2025 figures range from 27% out of school in Punjab to roughly 69% in Balochistan — yet Punjab's lower rate still conceals about 9.7 million children.

field.qualification: A share of units consumed is not a share of the subsidy bill or of cost recovery, and it says nothing about access quality — industry's smaller 31.5% may reflect a thin industrial base in an economy where agriculture is 23.44% of GDP, not restrained factory demand. It is also one fiscal year's metered grid consumption, so self-generation and unbilled losses sit outside the denominator.
field.hook: 47.5% vs 31.5% → homes outconsume factories by half again
field.useAgainst: "Electricity tariff reform is an industrial-competitiveness question, not a household-welfare one" — households are the single largest consuming category, so tariff design is distributional before it is industrial.
field.deploy: Energy pricing cannot be treated as an industrial-policy lever alone — households consumed about 47.5% of electricity in FY2025-26 against industry's 31.5%, the Pakistan Economic Survey reports, so reform's first-order effect is distributional rather than competitive.

field.qualification: Consumption measures electricity actually delivered and billed, not demand suppressed by load management or unaffordable tariffs, so 3.8% is a floor on unmet need rather than a measure of it. Against 2.07% population growth, the nine-month rise leaves per-head consumption up under 2% — recovery from a low base, not a demand boom.
field.hook: +3.8% in nine months → demand up, barely 1.7% per head
field.useAgainst: "Power demand is flat because the economy has stalled" — grid consumption grew 3.8% year-on-year in Jul-Mar FY2026, so the binding constraint is supply reliability and price, not absent demand.
field.deploy: The headline recovery in power demand is thinner than it looks. Electricity consumption grew about 3.8% in July–March FY2026 according to the Pakistan Economic Survey, but with population expanding 2.07% a year, per-head use barely moved.

field.qualification: A US$72m surplus is about 0.14% of the nine-month US$50.7bn import bill — a rounding margin one month of energy imports could erase, not a structural turn. It was delivered by US$30.3bn of remittances rather than by US$22.7bn of goods exports, so it records successful financing, not improved competitiveness.
field.hook: US$72m surplus → external balance held by a hair, not by exports
field.useAgainst: "The current-account surplus shows Pakistan has fixed its balance-of-payments problem" — a US$72m margin on US$50.7bn of imports is a knife-edge sustained by transfers, not a solved external account.
field.deploy: Stabilisation should not be mistaken for competitiveness: the Pakistan Economic Survey's US$72 million current-account surplus for July–March FY2026 rests on US$30.3 billion of remittances rather than on the US$22.7 billion earned from goods exports.

field.qualification: This is merchandise exports only for nine months — it excludes services and cannot be read against annual targets — and an absolute dollar level reveals nothing about product sophistication or unit value. Spread over 252.09m people it is roughly US$90 of goods exported per Pakistani in nine months, which is the real indictment.
field.hook: US$22.7bn in nine months → about $90 of goods exports per Pakistani
field.useAgainst: "Exports are the engine of Pakistan's recovery" — at US$22.7bn against a US$50.7bn import bill, exports cover under half the goods trade and are outstripped by remittances.
field.deploy: Pakistan's export base is small relative to the population it must support. The Pakistan Economic Survey records US$22.7 billion of goods exports in July–March FY2026, roughly US$90 for each of the country's 252.09 million people.

draftIssues: deploy cites figures not in fact/pairs: 90

field.qualification: The US$50.7bn covers goods only, so the true external gap is wider once services are added, and composition matters more than size: much of it is energy and intermediate inputs, which means import compression buys external balance by throttling industrial output. That a surplus coexisted with this bill shows the gap was financed, not narrowed.
field.hook: US$50.7bn → roughly $2.20 spent abroad for every $1 earned exporting
field.useAgainst: "The trade gap is closing under stabilisation" — imports of US$50.7bn against US$22.7bn of exports in the same nine months leave a merchandise gap larger than total exports.
field.deploy: Import compression buys external stability at the cost of industrial output, because the Pakistan Economic Survey's US$50.7 billion goods import bill for July–March FY2026 is dominated by energy and intermediate inputs that domestic producers cannot substitute.

field.qualification: Remittances are transfers earned abroad, not output produced at home: they finance consumption and reserves without adding domestic productive capacity, employment or technology. A rise in recorded flows can also reflect migration from informal channels into banks when the interbank and open-market rates converge, so higher formal remittances need not mean more money actually arriving.
field.hook: US$30.3bn in nine months → Pakistan's largest export is its workers
field.useAgainst: "Record remittances prove the economy is strengthening" — remittances rise when domestic labour markets fail, with unemployment up to 7.1% and 37% of 15-24s neither working nor studying.
field.deploy: Remittances are a symptom of domestic labour-market failure as much as a source of external strength; the US$30.3 billion recorded by the Pakistan Economic Survey in July–March FY2026 flows from workers who left an economy where unemployment climbed from 6.3% to 7.1%.

field.qualification: The ratio compares a transfer inflow with a production-based export, so it flatters remittances by construction: exports carry domestic value chains, wages and learning that remittances do not. It also rests on goods exports alone — counting services such as IT would narrow the gap — and covers nine months, not a full year.
field.hook: 1.33× → migrant earnings beat the whole goods-export machine by a third
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's external accounts rest on its export sector" — they rest on labour export, with nine-month remittances exceeding goods exports by roughly a third.
field.deploy: Pakistan has been more successful at exporting people than products: over July–March FY2026 remittances ran roughly a third larger than goods exports (Pakistan Economic Survey), while the working-age population swelled from about 159.8m in 2020-21 to 179.6m in 2024-25.

field.qualification: Reserves are a stock on one date, 15 May 2026, and are built from borrowing and transfers rather than earned export receipts, so the level can be bought and can be lost quickly. Against a nine-month import bill of US$50.7bn — about US$5.6bn a month — the SBP's US$17.1bn is roughly three months of cover, and the banks' US$5.5bn is not available to the central bank for intervention.
field.hook: US$17.1bn → about three months of imports, borrowed not earned
field.useAgainst: "Over US$22bn in reserves means the crisis is behind us" — three months of import cover absorbs one shock the size of the 2022 floods, then is gone.
field.deploy: Rebuilt reserves buy time without changing what Pakistan sells abroad. SBP holdings stood near US$17.1bn on 15 May 2026, with another US$5.5bn at commercial banks (Pakistan Economic Survey) — a stock accumulated largely through borrowing rather than export earnings.

field.qualification: This describes road links that exist on a map, not tonnage, transit revenue or trade actually crossing them — ADB's own corridor assessment says that transit trade remains limited in practice. Corridor membership also says nothing about who captures the gains: the routes run through provinces where poverty is deepest, and connectivity alone does not redistribute it.
field.hook: CAREC → Pakistan's roads already touch China, Kabul, Central Asia, Arabian Sea
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's geography automatically makes it the region's trade and transit hub" — corridor membership is a road network, not realised transit volume.
field.deploy: A corridor on a map is not income. CAREC ties Pakistan's roads to routes linking China, Afghanistan and Central Asia to the Arabian Sea (ADB), yet seven of the ten poorest districts in the World Bank's 2025 analysis sit in Balochistan.

field.qualification: ADB names transport/border infrastructure and costly cross-border services as constraints, but does not quantify the cost penalty or show that removing it would generate volumes — demand depends on Afghan and Central Asian trade, border closures and security, none of which a customs upgrade fixes. Note too that 'cross-border services' means freight, clearing and logistics firms, a sector where more than 85% of Pakistani employment is informal.
field.hook: Transit trade limited → borders and brokers, not maps, price the corridor
field.useAgainst: "Once the roads are built, regional trade will follow" — ADB identifies the binding constraint as border process and service costs, not tarmac.
field.deploy: The binding constraint on Pakistani transit is administrative, not geographic. ADB attributes persistently limited transit trade to poor transport and border infrastructure and costly cross-border services, performed in an economy where more than 85% of employment is informal (World Bank, 2025).

field.qualification: Climate-resilient sections and stronger NHA disaster-risk capacity are project components, not demonstrated performance — none of this has been tested against a 2022-scale flood, and hardening one highway does not protect the districts it passes through. Resilience here is engineering plus agency capacity, not an outcome measured in avoided losses.
field.hook: N55 climate-proofing → a corridor that washes away carries nothing
field.useAgainst: "Climate adaptation is a separate agenda from infrastructure and growth spending" — connectivity assets are themselves the exposed capital.
field.deploy: Climate risk now sets the lifespan of new infrastructure. ADB's CAREC investment accordingly funds climate-resilient N55 sections and stronger NHA disaster-risk capacity, though none of it has yet met a shock like the 2022 floods, which pushed another 13m Pakistanis into poverty (World Bank).

field.qualification: This is ADB's programme logic — its stated theory of change — not evidence that corridor investment has delivered growth, jobs or stability in Pakistan. The employment channel is the weakest link: past labour absorption ran into low-productivity construction, trade and transport, exactly the sectors corridor spending expands.
field.hook: Economic Corridors Programme → roads sold as growth, jobs, trade and stability
field.useAgainst: "Corridor investment converts directly into productive employment" — the last labour shift went mostly into low-productivity construction, trade and transport.
field.deploy: The weak link in corridor-led development is employment. ADB's Pakistan Economic Corridors Programme ties connectivity investment to growth, jobs, regional trade and stability, yet labour absorption has run into low-productivity construction, trade and transport, with 37% of Pakistanis aged 15-24 NEET (World Bank, 2025).

field.qualification: An approval date and a 37-month calendar measure intent, not delivery: the arrangement runs to roughly October 2027 only if every review passes, and Pakistan's IMF history includes arrangements approved and never drawn at all. Approval is also not money — the disbursed total is a separate figure.
field.hook: 37 months from 25 Sep 2024 → stabilisation measured in years, not tranches
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan has secured an IMF bailout, so the crisis is over" — approval starts a multi-year, review-by-review reform programme.
field.deploy: An approval date measures intent, not delivery. The IMF approved Pakistan's 37-month Extended Fund Facility on 25 September 2024, yet cumulative EFF and RSF disbursements stood at only about US$4.8bn by 8 May 2026.

field.qualification: The commitment is denominated in SDR 5.32bn; the ~US$7bn is a conversion at approval in September 2024 and drifts with the SDR rate, so quoting it as a fixed dollar sum in a later year is wrong. It is also a ceiling released in tranches over 37 months, set against a goods import bill of roughly US$50.7bn in nine months alone.
field.hook: SDR 5.32bn ≈ US$7bn → a three-year ceiling, not cash in hand
field.useAgainst: "The US$7bn programme covers Pakistan's external financing needs" — it is a phased ceiling, small beside the import and reserve numbers it is meant to backstop.
field.deploy: A commitment ceiling is not cash in hand: Pakistan's EFF is denominated at SDR 5.32bn, roughly US$7bn at approval in 2024 (IMF), while EFF and RSF disbursements reached about US$4.8bn by 8 May 2026 — set against US$50.7bn of goods imports in nine months.

field.qualification: The RSF is a separate 28-month facility with its own reform measures and a shorter clock than the 37-month EFF, so its SDR1bn accrues only as climate-related measures are completed, not on approval. At under a fifth of the EFF commitment, it is a policy signal about where conditionality now reaches, not a scale of climate finance.
field.hook: SDR1bn, 28 months → IMF conditionality now priced for climate risk
field.useAgainst: "IMF programmes are purely about fiscal austerity and ignore climate" — a dedicated resilience facility now sits alongside the EFF.
field.deploy: Climate conditionality has arrived as leverage rather than volume: the IMF's Resilience and Sustainability Facility, approved in May 2025, commits SDR1bn over 28 months, a shorter clock than the 37-month EFF approved on 25 September 2024.

field.qualification: This is a cumulative total across two facilities at one date — EFF plus RSF — so it cannot be read as EFF progress alone, and it is gross inflow to the sovereign, not net external financing once repayments to the Fund are counted. Against SBP reserves of about US$17.1bn in May 2026, it is a buffer contribution, not a balance-of-payments solution.
field.hook: US$4.8bn by 8 May 2026 → disbursed, not the US$7bn headline
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan has received US$7bn from the IMF" — the approved ceiling and the amount actually drawn are different numbers.
field.deploy: Fund money buys time rather than solvency. The IMF records cumulative EFF and RSF disbursements of about US$4.8bn by 8 May 2026, set against SBP reserves of roughly US$17.1bn on 15 May 2026 and US$5.5bn more held by commercial banks.

field.qualification: This is an association reported in government analysis, not a causal estimate: educated mothers in Pakistan are also disproportionately urban and better-off, so facility access and income are doing part of the work attributed to schooling. The government's own antenatal figures show where education stops mattering — roughly 88% get prenatal consultation and 84% a skilled birth attendant, but postnatal care collapses to about 44%, a supply-side gap no amount of maternal schooling closes.
field.hook: Educate a girl → maternal and public-health returns collected a generation later
field.useAgainst: 'Girls' schooling is a welfare expenditure, not a health intervention' — government analysis treats female education as a determinant of maternal and public-health outcomes, making it health spending under another budget line.
field.deploy: Female schooling shifts what households do, not what clinics can offer. Government of Pakistan analysis in 2026 links it to better maternal and public-health outcomes, yet postnatal care in the same year reached only about 44%.

field.qualification: Exports-to-GDP is a ratio with two moving parts: it can fall while export dollars rise, simply because nominal GDP (inflated domestic prices, a large non-traded services and construction sector) grows faster. The 'historical peak' is also whatever the study period contains, not a policy target, and the ratio excludes remittances, so it measures export orientation rather than total FX earning capacity.
field.hook: 16% → under 10%: exports are a shrinking slice of a growing economy
field.useAgainst: 'Pakistan's recurring dollar crises are an import-bill problem' — the import side is only half the ratio; the export denominator has been eroding for a decade, which is why every growth spurt ends at the SBP reserves counter.
field.deploy: Growth in Pakistan has been financed by everything except exports — the World Bank tracks exports-to-GDP falling from a historical peak near 16% to below 10%, while much labour reallocation ran into low-productivity construction, trade and transport (2025).

field.qualification: The 26% gap is measured before these firms exported, so it identifies self-selection, not any benefit of exporting — it tells you who clears the threshold, not what crossing it does. The comparison also runs only over firms that eventually succeeded in exporting, so productive firms that tried and failed are absent, and the universe is formal firms with usable accounts, a sliver of an economy that is over 85% informal.
field.hook: 26% → exporters were already better before they ever shipped abroad
field.useAgainst: 'Give ordinary firms an export subsidy and they will become exporters' — the productivity gap exists before entry, so a rebate cheque cannot manufacture an exporter out of a firm that was never near the threshold.
field.deploy: Export promotion aimed at market access targets the wrong constraint, since World Bank analysis finds future exporters already 26% more productive than firms that never exported, and such schemes reach only formal firms in an economy over 85% informal (2025).

field.qualification: Controls remove observable differences, not unobserved ones: management quality, family capital and buyer relationships plausibly drive both sustained exporting and the 21% premium, so part of what looks like learning-by-exporting is still selection into staying an exporter. Note also that 'systematic' versus 'latent' classifies the regularity of exporting, not its volume — the premium attaches to consistency, so an occasional large shipment does not buy it.
field.hook: 21% → staying in export markets keeps teaching, it doesn't only select
field.useAgainst: 'Exporting only reflects productivity, it never creates it, so trade openness is a sideshow' — the premium that survives after controls says integration itself is a productivity channel, not merely a sorting mechanism.
field.deploy: If integration teaches anything, it rewards regularity: after controls, systematic exporters were 21% more productive than latent exporters in World Bank analysis, a premium attaching to consistency of exporting rather than to the occasional large shipment.

field.qualification: This is a level comparison, not evidence of spillover: foreign firms cluster in capital-intensive, often protected segments, so a 46% premium is fully compatible with zero transfer to domestic suppliers. Causation also runs backwards — multinationals acquire the best domestic firms, so some of the premium was there before the foreign ownership was.
field.hook: 46% → foreign-owned firms outproduce domestic twins; linkage decides who benefits
field.useAgainst: 'FDI is repatriated profit with no productive content for the host economy' — the measured productivity gap is exactly the capital, management and knowledge that domestic linkage policy is supposed to capture.
field.deploy: FDI is only as valuable as the linkages built around it, and foreign-owned firms were about 46% more productive than comparable domestic firms in World Bank analysis — a gap that sits comfortably inside cities the Bank calls, in parts, 'sterile agglomeration' (2025).

field.qualification: The universe is listed firms — a few hundred large, formal companies — so this tracks the export behaviour of the most capable end of the economy and says nothing about unlisted SMEs or the informal majority. The share can also fall without any exporter quitting, if the exchange lists new domestically-focused firms (banks, cement, utilities) that dilute the denominator.
field.hook: 60%→51% → roughly one in seven listed exporters left world markets
field.useAgainst: 'Export stagnation is entirely a demand problem in our buyer markets' — firms withdrew from exporting during the same period, which is a participation failure at home, not an order book failure abroad.
field.deploy: Whatever ails Pakistan's exports operates inside the boardrooms of its largest companies, where the share of listed firms exporting fell from roughly 60% to 51% over the decade the World Bank studied.

field.qualification: Exports-to-sales falls whenever domestic sales grow faster, so an import-substituting home boom drags the ratio down without a single dollar of exports being lost — the figure measures orientation, not export value. It is also computed only over firms still exporting, so the firms that exited entirely are excluded, meaning it understates rather than captures the full aggregate retreat.
field.hook: 31%→27% → even surviving exporters now sell more at home
field.useAgainst: 'Our existing exporters are maxed out; we only need more of them' — intensity fell among incumbent exporters too, so the constraint sits inside surviving firms, not just in the count of participants.
field.deploy: The export slowdown runs deeper than lost firms: World Bank figures show exports' share of sales among listed exporters falling some 31% to 27%, even as much labour shifted in 2025 into low-productivity construction, trade and transport.

field.qualification: Proximity is geographic potential, not realised trade: map distance prices in nothing about corridor security, border closures, transit agreements or port turnaround, and the hinterland markets involved — Afghanistan and Central Asia — are small economies, so shortest access is not the same as large volumes. This is ADB's characterisation of location, not a measurement of transit tonnage or transit revenue earned.
field.hook: Shortest ocean door → for Kabul, Central Asia and western China alike
field.useAgainst: 'Pakistan is peripheral to global trade routes and can only compete on cheap labour' — it holds the closest sea access for three landlocked hinterlands, an asset that is unearned but perishable if corridors stay insecure.
field.deploy: Geography has handed Pakistan an asset few states possess: the ADB notes it offers some of the closest sea access to Afghanistan, Central Asia and western China — yet seven of the ten poorest districts in the World Bank's 2025 analysis lie in Balochistan.

field.qualification: The 9.7m is a function of Punjab being by far the largest province: at a 27% rate it excludes a smaller share of its 5-16 cohort than Sindh, KP or Balochistan, so the number is not evidence that Punjab's system performs worst. It also lumps never-enrolled children with dropouts, so it is not a single queue of 9.7m children waiting for seats.
field.hook: 9.7m → Pakistan's biggest out-of-school population sits in its lowest-rate province
field.useAgainst: "Fix Balochistan and you fix Pakistan's out-of-school crisis" — Punjab alone carries ~9.7m of the 25.1m, against Balochistan's 3.5m.
field.deploy: Any national plan to reopen the classroom door must start in Punjab, where UNICEF counts roughly 9.7m out-of-school children in 2025 — a far larger absolute burden than Balochistan's, even though Punjab's 27% exclusion rate is the country's lowest.

field.qualification: These counts rank provinces by the size of their child populations as much as by exclusion: Balochistan is smallest in absolute terms (3.5m) yet worst in rate (~69%), so the league table inverts depending on which measure you pick. All four figures cover only the 5-16 band, so pre-primary and post-16 exclusion sits outside them entirely.
field.hook: 3.5m → Balochistan's smallest count, highest exclusion rate: size is not severity
field.useAgainst: "Sindh's 7.4m makes it Pakistan's worst performer on schooling" — its 44% rate is well under Balochistan's ~69%; the 7.4m reflects population size.
field.deploy: Budgets cannot simply follow headcount. UNICEF's 2025 figures put Sindh's out-of-school children at about 7.4m, KP's at 4.5m and Balochistan's at 3.5m, yet Balochistan — smallest in number — excludes nearly 69% of its children.

field.qualification: This is UNICEF's identification of a barrier, not a measured effect size: it attaches no number to how many of the 25.1m out-of-school children would return under reliable power. Unreliable electricity also travels with poverty, remoteness and weak school infrastructure, so it cannot be isolated as an independent cause of non-attendance.
field.hook: No reliable power → attendance, retention and learning all break before pedagogy does
field.useAgainst: "Out-of-school numbers are a schools-and-teachers problem" — UNICEF ties attendance, retention and learning losses to unreliable electricity, an energy-sector failure.
field.deploy: Load-shedding belongs in the education debate, not only the energy one: UNICEF observed in 2025 that unreliable electricity obstructs attendance, retention and learning, the same year the World Bank found 78% of ten-year-olds unable to read a simple text.

field.qualification: 288,000 is an output count of learners reached by UNICEF-supported interventions, not children shown to have acquired foundational skills; the 54,000 ECE figure is a subset, not an addition. Set against 25.1m out-of-school children and 78% of ten-year-olds unable to read a simple text, it is proof of concept at roughly 1% scale, not coverage.
field.hook: 288,000 supported → pilot-scale remedy facing a 78% reading-failure problem
field.useAgainst: "Donor-backed learning programmes are closing Pakistan's learning gap" — 288,000 learners, 54,000 of them in ECE, is a fraction of the affected cohort.
field.deploy: Pilot success and national repair are different orders of magnitude: UNICEF-supported interventions delivered foundational-learning support to 288,000 learners in 2025, including 54,000 in early childhood education, against 25.1m children aged 5-16 still out of school.

field.qualification: "Prenatal consultation" records that contact with a provider happened, not how many visits, how early, or whether anything clinically useful was done; it covers only women captured in the reported indicators. The same women's postnatal coverage at ~44% shows this contact does not carry past delivery.
field.hook: 88% → almost every pregnancy meets a provider before delivery, few after
field.useAgainst: "Pakistani women have no access to maternal healthcare" — about 88% received a prenatal consultation; the failure is continuity, not first contact.
field.deploy: Pakistan's maternal health system reaches women before birth and loses them after it: government figures for 2026 record about 88% receiving prenatal consultation and 84% of births attended by skilled professionals, but postnatal care covering only 44%.

field.qualification: This tracks a single campaign-deliverable injection among women in the maternal indicators — the easiest class of service to scale — and says nothing about routine child immunisation or completion of multi-dose schedules. The same system's postnatal coverage of ~44% shows the reach does not transfer to services needing repeat visits.
field.hook: 86% → single-contact prevention scales in Pakistan; multi-visit care does not
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's health system cannot deliver anything at scale" — about 86% tetanus coverage shows one-contact preventive services do reach most women.
field.deploy: What the state can deliver in a single visit, it delivers well: tetanus vaccination reached roughly 86% of women in the government's 2026 indicators, yet postnatal care — which requires a return journey — reached only 44%.

field.qualification: Skilled attendance counts a qualified professional being present at delivery; it does not establish that emergency obstetric care, blood supply or referral was available if labour went wrong. It is also a national average across provinces whose other service indicators diverge sharply, and attendance at birth is not care continued — postnatal follow-up reaches only ~44%.
field.hook: 84% → skilled hands at delivery, no guarantee of emergency care behind them
field.useAgainst: "Most Pakistani women still deliver without any trained attendant" — about 84% of births are attended by a skilled health professional.
field.deploy: Government investment in frontline delivery has produced measurable gains, with roughly 84% of births now attended by a skilled health professional according to Government of Pakistan figures for 2026 — a base on which continuity of care, not access, becomes the binding problem.

field.qualification: The 44% is a coverage share only: it does not record when after delivery the contact occurred or what was provided, and without mortality data it cannot be presented as the cause of maternal deaths. Its argumentative force comes entirely from the contrast with the ~84-88% reached before and during birth — a drop-off in continuity, not an absence of services.
field.hook: 44% → maternal care stops at the delivery-room door
field.useAgainst: "High antenatal and skilled-birth coverage shows Pakistan's maternal pathway works" — fewer than half of women receive any postnatal care.
field.deploy: Coverage in Pakistan collapses the moment the delivery ends; the Government of Pakistan's 2026 figures put postnatal care at roughly 44%, against about 88% for prenatal consultation and 84% for skilled attendance at birth.

field.qualification: An arrangement approved is not money used: the SDR25m 1958 SBA was never drawn, so it evidences access to Fund resources, not balance-of-payments rescue. It also sets no scale precedent — SDR25m is trivially small beside the SDR5.32bn 2024 EFF, so the 1958 date marks the start of the relationship, not of dependence.
field.hook: SDR25m in 1958, nothing drawn → access arranged, not rescue taken
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan has been living off IMF money continuously since the 1950s" — the very first arrangement was a precautionary standby from which not a rupee was drawn.
field.deploy: Pakistan's engagement with the Fund opened with a commitment nobody used: on the IMF's record of historical arrangements, the SDR25m stand-by approved on 8 December 1958 was never drawn, a sum trivial beside the SDR5.32bn Extended Fund Facility of 2024.

field.qualification: The 21% is a share of the analysed population in selected climate- and conflict-vulnerable districts, not of Pakistan's population, so it cannot be read as a national hunger rate; the 7.5m is also a projection for one Dec–Mar window, not an annual average. Because the district set analysed changes between rounds, the headline share is not directly comparable year to year.
field.hook: 7.5m in Phase 3+ → one in five in analysed districts, not nationwide
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan produces a wheat surplus, so food security is essentially solved" — availability at national level coexists with 7.5m people in acute crisis in the analysed districts.
field.deploy: Climate shocks translate directly into hunger in Pakistan's most exposed districts, where the IPC projects some 7.5m people — 21% of the population analysed — in Phase 3 or worse between December 2025 and March 2026.

field.qualification: The ~US$11.5bn is two-way goods and services combined, so it says nothing about the direction of the balance, the composition of what is traded, or whether the flows are concentrated in a few low-value-added lines. It is a single-year 2025 USTR total, and a trade volume is not the same as investment, technology transfer or strategic alignment.
field.hook: US$11.5bn two-way → the US link survives as commerce, both directions counted
field.useAgainst: "After the Afghanistan drawdown the US-Pakistan relationship has no substance left" — the commercial leg still carried roughly US$11.5bn in goods and services in 2025.
field.deploy: A relationship usually read through security has a commercial floor beneath it. USTR recorded about US$11.5bn in two-way goods and services trade with Pakistan in 2025, a volume figure that says nothing about balance or composition.

field.qualification: Full membership from 9 June 2017 is a seat at a consensus-based forum, not leverage inside it, and the date alone shows nothing about what Pakistan has extracted from membership in trade, connectivity or security terms. The twelve-year wait from observer status in 2005 is itself the point: accession was slow and negotiated, so membership marks the beginning of a bargaining process rather than its result.
field.hook: Observer 2005 → member 2017: twelve years bought a seat, not a settlement
field.useAgainst: "Pakistan's Eurasian turn is a recent improvisation after US disengagement" — the SCO track ran from observer status in 2005 to full membership in 2017, long predating it.
field.deploy: Pakistan's Eurasian alignment was negotiated slowly rather than declared: MOFA and SCO records date observer status to 2005 and full Shanghai Cooperation Organisation membership to 9 June 2017, a seat at a consensus forum rather than leverage within it.
